sens: Place where a body is buried, a grave
Action of burying someone, interment
Honor or dishonor given to a dead person by their burial
H6900.detail:
1. The tomb is primarily the physical place, the grave itself where a body rests: it is an excavation, a cavity dug in the ground or in rock. Jacob raises a monument on Rachel's tomb to mark it (Genesis 35:20), and King Josiah is buried in his own tomb, that of the kings of David (2 Kings 23:30).
2. The word also refers to the act of burying, the interment itself. Genesis 47:30 shows a dying man pleading to be buried in the land of his fathers, and Deuteronomy 34:6 recounts that the Lord buried Moses in a valley, without a witness.
3. Finally, having a burial or not becomes a symbol of dignity or shame. One who receives an honorable burial joins their ancestors (2 Kings 9:28); one who does not—cast out as Jeremiah prophesies for King Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 22:19)—suffers ultimate dishonor. Ecclesiastes 6:3 shows that a long and rich life is empty without a worthy burial.
H6900.origine: The Hebrew word קְבֻרָה (qeburah) comes from the root קָבַר (qabar), "to bury." This root evokes the action of covering, of burying underground. It appears dozens of times in the Hebrew Bible to describe interment. The name qeburah designates both the act and the place, as is often the case in Hebrew. It is a fundamental concept in biblical culture: having a burial at home, in the land of one's fathers, is a sacred right.
H6900.emploi: The word qeburah ("tomb") appears 13 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical and wisdom books. In Genesis, it refers to family tombs: Genesis 35:20 and 47:30 show the importance of being buried near one's parents. In Kings and Chronicles, it describes royal burial as a dynastic honor (2 Kings 9:28, 23:30; 2 Chronicles 26:23). Ecclesiastes 6:3 uses it philosophically: lacking a burial is compared to a curse worse than dying prematurely. Jeremiah 22:19 sees it as the ultimate sign of divine judgment on Jehoiakim. In the oracles against the nations (Isaiah 14:20, Ezekiel 32), being deprived of burial is the punishment for the wicked or defeated enemies.
H6900.portee: For the biblical believer, this word reveals the spiritual importance of the body and the respect for the dead. A worthy burial is not a luxury but a human necessity, linked to honor and memory. It also expresses the promise of being gathered to one's ancestors—a form of hope. Conversely, being deprived of burial was feared as a final curse, which helps to understand why Jesus himself, although crucified as a criminal, had to be buried in a respectable tomb to fulfill the Scriptures.

sens: To take something that is given or brought to you
To accept, agree to, consent to
To correspond, fit together
H6901.detail:
1. To receive is to take in hand what is presented to you: the Levites receive the gold and silver from the offerings to take to the temple (Ezra 8:30), or the blood of the sacrifices to sprinkle on the altar (2 Chronicles 29:22). It is a concrete act of taking possession.
2. To accept goes further: it is to receive while giving your assent. When David welcomes the warriors who come to help him, he receives and accepts them into his army (1 Chronicles 12:18). It is to receive with kindness.
3. To correspond or fit together: in the tabernacle, the laces of the two linen panels corresponded to each other, like two pieces that fit together (Exodus 26:5). Here, to receive means "to adapt to" or "to be facing".
4. To receive can also mean "to welcome misfortune": Job receives the blows from the Lord, accepting them as just (Job 2:10). It is to receive with resignation.
H6901.origine: The Hebrew verb קָבַל (qabal) comes from a root that evokes the idea of "facing" or "going towards." Its primary meaning is to take face-to-face, to welcome what comes towards you. In biblical Hebrew, this verb is close to the idea of receiving a visit or consenting to something. Its Aramaic equivalent, קַבֵּל (qabel), has the same meaning.
H6901.emploi: The verb qabal appears about a dozen times in the Hebrew Bible. It is first used for the concrete action of receiving: receiving offerings (Ezra 8:30), receiving blood (2 Chronicles 29:22), receiving impurities (2 Chronicles 29:16). It is also used for welcoming kindly: receiving allies (1 Chronicles 12:18) or receiving with assent (Esther 9:23 and 9:27, where the Jews receive an observance). A particular usage appears in the description of the tabernacle, where the laces "corresponded" to each other (Exodus 26:5, 36:12), giving the verb the technical sense of "being face to face" or "fitting together." This last usage shows that to receive can mean "to be in correspondence with."
H6901.portee: This word shows us that receiving is not a passive attitude. The Bible presents reception as an act: accepting the good things that God or others offer us, but also accepting His will, even when it involves suffering. To receive is to consent, to come into agreement with what is entrusted to us. For the believer, this speaks of welcoming God's grace and word.

sens: To take possession of something that is given or offered to you
To obtain, acquire power or authority
To accept, welcome something from God
H6902.detail:
1. To receive a gift or reward: it is to take in hand what is handed to you. The wise men of Babylon receive gifts and honors from the king if they reveal the dream (Daniel 2:6)—a simple transaction from person to person.
2. To seize a kingdom or position: to receive means here to take possession of a charge, of power (Daniel 5:31, Darius seizes the kingdom). It is to receive something of importance, an authority that passes from one hand to another.
3. To receive from God an eternal inheritance: the saints receive the kingdom from the hands of the Most High (Daniel 7:18)—not by usurpation, but as a gift granted by God Himself, guaranteeing an everlasting reign.
H6902.origine: This Aramaic verb (the dialect of parts of Daniel and Ezra) comes from the same root as the Hebrew verb קָבַל (qabál, "to receive") from the Old Testament. The basic image is that of taking, seizing, welcoming. The root is also found in the name "Qabbalah" (the Jewish esoteric tradition), which literally means "reception." In Aramaic, the form used here is the Pael (equivalent to the Hebrew Piel), which reinforces or specifies the action.
H6902.emploi: The verb appears three times in the book of Daniel, which is partially written in Aramaic. It first designates a remuneration or a gift (Daniel 2:6); then, the accession to political power (Daniel 5:31); finally, and most importantly theologically, the inheritance of the kingdom that God reserves for the saints (Daniel 7:18). In this last context, the verb takes on its full significance: to receive does not mean to conquer by force, but to welcome what the Most High decides to grant. It is the same root as in Hebrew, but limited here to the Aramaic passages of Daniel.
H6902.portee: This word reminds us that our relationship with God is not transactional or based on our merits. To receive the kingdom is to recognize that it is a gift, not something owed. For the believer, this invites us to receive with gratitude and humility what God offers, rather than pretending to conquer or earn it by ourselves. It is also a promise: despite trials and human empires, the kingdom of the saints is assured by divine will.

sens: Position in front, face to face
In the presence of, under the eyes of
Because of, due to
According to, in accordance with
H6903G.detail:
1. The primary meaning is spatial: what is in front, ahead of something or someone. In Daniel 2:31, King Nebuchadnezzar sees a great statue "before" him, meaning face to face, visible to his eyes.

2. From this spatial meaning arises the idea of being in the presence of someone, under their gaze or authority. In Daniel 3:3, the satraps place themselves "before" the statue of the king, that is, in his presence, thus marking their submission. Similarly, in Daniel 5:1, the king drinks wine "in the presence" of his nobles (the word literally means "before" them).

3. The word takes on a causal meaning: "because of," "due to." In Ezra 4:16, the adversaries say that "by" this (that is, because of the reconstruction of the city), the king will lose his possession. It is because the city will be rebuilt that danger threatens.

4. It can also mean "according to," "in accordance with." In Ezra 6:13, the governors act according to the king Darius's "order," that is, in conformity with what he commanded.
H6903G.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally evokes the idea of "face" or "in front." The same root produces other words related to presence, confrontation, or face. It is a common word in late Aramaic and Hebrew texts (particularly in the books of Ezra and Daniel, which contain sections in Aramaic). The basic image is concrete: what stands face to face with someone.
H6903G.emploi: This word appears 7 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the books of Ezra and Daniel (Aramaic sections). It functions as a preposition and conjunction, depending on the context. Sometimes it expresses a spatial position ("before the statue"), sometimes a presence ("in the presence of"), sometimes a cause ("because of"), and sometimes conformity ("according to"). The political and ceremonial context of the narratives (dedications of statues, royal decrees, feasts) often highlights the idea of official presence or authority: being "before" the king or the statue means being under his authority.
H6903G.portee: This word reminds the reader that in the Bible, being "before" God or a king means much more than physical proximity: it is to be under the gaze, under the authority, responsible. When speaking of statues or idols "before" which one stands, it raises the question of worship and allegiance. For the believer, the word invites reflection on what it means to stand "before" the living God.

sens: cause or reason for a fact
consequence of an action or event
circumstance that explains a context
foundation or motive
H6903H.detail:
1. The most direct meaning is **cause**: why something happens. Daniel 2:8 illustrates this well: the king says to the wise men, "I perceive that you want to gain time, because you see that the matter has escaped me" — he states the reason for their behavior.
2. The word also expresses **consequence** or what follows from it. In Daniel 2:41, the prophet says, "this kingdom will be divided; but there will be in it something of the strength of iron, because you saw the iron mixed with clay" — he links the effect to its origin.
3. Sometimes it simply marks the **context** or **occasion** of an event, without strict causal link. In Daniel 3:8, "At that time, some Chaldeans approached" — the word marks the moment and environment rather than a logical cause.
4. It can also mean **in relation to** or **facing**, indicating the motive or interest: in Ezra 4:14, "as we eat the salt of the palace" (which creates an obligation to the king) shows the foundation of a responsibility.
H6903H.origine: This Aramaic word comes from a root meaning "front" or "face," hence the idea of what stands **before** you. From there, the meaning of "in front of," "against," then "because of" and finally "because" develops. The transition from the concrete (the face, the front) to the abstract (the reason) is a very natural figure: what faces you, what opposes you, or what you see is often the **cause** that motivates your action.
H6903H.emploi: This word appears 22 times in biblical Aramaic, concentrated almost entirely in the books of Daniel and Ezra (the sections written in Aramaic in the New Testament are mostly in Western Aramaic). It serves to link one proposition to another to show the causal or contextual relationship. In Daniel 2:8, 2:41, 5:12, it clearly states the **cause** of a situation. In Daniel 2:12 and 3:8, it sometimes appears in the formula "thereupon" or "on this occasion," marking more the **logical sequence** or the **moment** than pure causality. In Ezra 4:14 and 7:17, it specifies the **motive** or **reason** for a decision. The word thus has a certain flexibility: it can be strictly causal or more broadly explanatory, even chronological.
H6903H.portee: For the Christian reader, this word invites us to see how events hold together: how God weaves causes and consequences to fulfill His plan. In reading the narratives of Daniel, where "because" recurs constantly, we discover that **behind every event lies a reason**, often the faithfulness of God's servants or the power of God Himself. This teaches us that our lives are not chaos: every action has its fruits, and God sees the entire chain.

sens: Siege instrument consisting of a massive beam mounted on a rolling device, used to break down the walls of fortresses
H6904.detail: 1. The ram is a war machine designed to demolish walls during a siege. It is a heavy beam, often fitted with a metal head, that is repeatedly thrust against walls to break them. In the text of Ezekiel, the prophet describes Nebuchadnezzar directing the blows of his ram against the walls of Tyre: the image is one of brute and determined force striking relentlessly to destroy.
H6904.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "one who goes before" or "one who precedes" — the ram is indeed the device that opens the way, that precedes the final assault by breaking down defenses. The idea of something that thrusts forward, striking head-on, is at the heart of the word.
H6904.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 26:9, in the prophecy of the destruction of Tyre by the king of Babylon. It is a very concrete image of the military techniques of the ancient Near East: the Assyrians and Babylonians perfected the use of the ram to reduce fortified cities. This technical vocabulary of sieges shows the extent and reality of the threat looming over Tyre.
H6904.portee: This word reminds us of the destructive power of God's judgment. Tyre, proud of its walls and wealth, will not be able to withstand the irresistible force He will send against it. It is a lesson on the vanity of human defenses in the face of divine will.

sens: in front of, in the presence of
under the eyes of, publicly
H6905H.detail:
1. This Hebrew word expresses the position or relationship of one thing placed face to another, "in front of." In 2 Kings 15:10, Shallum strikes the king "before the people": the action takes place in direct presence of witnesses, visible to all.
2. By extension, "before" means "in the presence of" or "publicly," emphasizing that the act is not hidden but carried out openly, under the gaze of all. Striking someone "before the people" means doing so ostentatiously, without concealment.
H6905H.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of position in front of a person or thing. It is very close to the Aramaic qevel (קֳבֵל) which also means "before." The Hebrew preposition first evokes physical space, then extends to the figurative sense: to be "before" someone is to be in their presence.
H6905H.emploi: This word appears only once in the Segond translations, in 2 Kings 15:10, where it describes how Shallum kills King Zachariah in the presence of the people. In this historical context of political assassination, "before the people" emphasizes the public and deliberate nature of the crime. The preposition situates the action in a social and public framework, not in secrecy.
H6905H.portee: This word reminds us that certain acts, particularly violence and injustices, cannot remain hidden when they are publicly committed. Being "before the people" means that all witnesses remain responsible for what they see.

sens: To strip someone of their goods or what belongs to them
To defraud by withholding or refusing what is owed
To disappoint or frustrate someone in their rights
H6906.detail:
1. The basic meaning is to strip: to take from someone what belongs to them, to deprive them of their goods. In Proverbs 22:23, the Lord defends the one who is "stripped" — it is the brutal act of stealing or taking away their resources.
2. The word is mainly used to deceive in religious duty: to fraudulently refuse or withhold what is owed to God. In Malachi 3:8-9, Israel "deceives" the Lord by refusing tithes and offerings — it is a form of spiritual theft, a betrayal in giving.
3. More broadly, it is to frustrate or betray someone's trust: to deprive them of what they legally or justly expect from us.
H6906.origine: The Hebrew root קבע suggests the idea of stripping or depriving. The verb is infrequent and its exact etymology remains uncertain, but its use in prophetic texts connects it to the moral and religious domain: to deceive is primarily a failure in duty towards God or towards one's neighbor.
H6906.emploi: This verb appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, always with a nuance of fraud or theft. In Proverbs 22:23, it refers to the one who is stripped, a victim of injustice. In Malachi 3:8-9, the prophet uses it three times: Israel deceives God by refusing tithes and offerings. This is the central accusation of the prophet: the people deliberately withhold what they owe to the Lord, and this betrayal of trust brings upon them a curse. The religious and ethical context dominates everywhere.
H6906.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to faithfulness and integrity. Not to deceive God or one's neighbor is to respect the duty of justice and trust. Malachi's warning reminds us that refusing God what is due to Him — whether it be giving, obedience, or sincerity — is a form of theft that carries consequences. It is a call to examine our hearts: are we faithful in the small things as well as in the great ones?

sens: Container holding a drink that makes one insensitive or intoxicated
Image of God's anger and judgment that nations must drink
Inevitable suffering imposed by God on the one who receives it
H6907.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a cup, a vessel intended for drinking. But in Isaiah, it is not a simple glass: it is a cup filled with a drink that stupefies, that makes one feel drunk or unconscious. This image evokes a potion that paralyzes, that takes away the clarity from the one who drinks it.
2. In Isaiah 51:22, the Lord tells Jerusalem that He will take from His hand the cup of her staggering, the cup of His anger. The Bible often speaks this way: to drink the cup of God means to undergo His judgment, His punishment. Jerusalem had drunk this cup and was like dazed — it had suffered the misfortunes of divine judgment.
3. More broadly, this cup represents a suffering or punishment that God imposes and that cannot be avoided: the one who must drink it must drink it. It is inevitable, like a rendered judgment.
H6907.origine: The Hebrew word qubba'at comes from the root meaning "cup" or "container." The image of the "cup" is very ancient in the East: to drink a cup meant to receive what was given to you to drink, whether it be an honor, a remedy, or a punishment. In the Bible, the cup becomes the favorite image of judgment and the fate imposed by God.
H6907.emploi: This word appears only twice, both in the same passage in Isaiah (51:17 and 51:22), where it describes the situation of Jerusalem under God's judgment. In verse 51:17, the city has drunk the cup of staggering and is reeling under its weight. In verse 51:22, the Lord promises to take this cup from the hands of the people: He will cease punishing them and will give its contents to the oppressors. The word expresses the idea that the people, intoxicated by suffering, will be delivered.
H6907.portee: This image speaks to our experience: we all know moments when we feel overwhelmed by difficulties, as if dazed by suffering. The text teaches us that our trials are not eternal — God can take the cup from our hands. It also invites us to recognize that some sufferings may be the result of divine judgment, and that deliverance comes from Him alone.

sens: To bring together scattered or dispersed things in one place
To unite people into one group or assembly
To accumulate goods, wealth by gathering
To regroup scattered peoples or nations
To collect, gather something precious
H6908.detail:
1. To gather scattered material objects: it is to put together what was separated. In Genesis 41:35, Joseph asks that they "gather" the grains of the good harvests into the granaries, as one piles up wheat for preservation.
2. To gather people to form a group: it is to call the people to join together for a common action. In 2 Samuel 2:25, the sons of Benjamin "rallied" to Abner, forming a united troop.
3. To accumulate wealth gradually: it is to save, to capitalize. In Proverbs 13:11, it speaks of wealth that one "gathers" gradually through saving.
4. To bring together a dispersed people: it is to restore the unity of a fragmented nation. In Ezekiel 29:13, God promises to "gather" the Egyptians whom He has scattered among the nations.
5. To collect, gather offerings or contributions: it is to seek and gather what one needs. In 2 Chronicles 24:5, they "collect" money for the repair of the temple.
H6908.origine: The verb קָבַץ comes from a root that expresses the idea of compression and grouping. It is close to Semitic roots describing the action of tightening, binding together, or pressing. The word fundamentally designates the movement that gathers and unifies what was dispersed or separated.
H6908.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the Old Testament (121 occurrences) and is found in all narrative and prophetic contexts. It describes both the gathering of material goods (harvests in Genesis 41, wealth in Proverbs) and of people (military troops, civil or religious assemblies). In prophetic context, especially in Isaiah and Jeremiah, it often expresses messianic hope: the regathering of exiles scattered among the nations, and their return to communal life. The verb carries the idea of restoring broken unity.
H6908.portee: This word speaks to the believer about the reality of human dispersion — we are often divided, fragmented, scattered by sin and distance. But it also proclaims a major hope: God is the one who gathers His people, who restores unity. It is a promise particularly dear to exiles and to all those who feel distant or lost. The gathering in Jesus Christ, in His Church, thus becomes the fulfillment of this ancient promise.

sens: City of Judah in the southeast, near Edom
H6909.detail: Kabtseel is the southernmost and easternmost city in the territory of Judah, mentioned at the top of the list of cities in the Negev (the desert south). It was located on the border of Edom, in an inhospitable region. It is from this remote city that Benaja, one of King David's chief warriors, originates (2 Samuel 23:20 and 1 Chronicles 11:22).
H6909.origine: The name Kabtseel literally means "God gathers" (in Hebrew: God + gathers). It is a promise or an affirmation: even at the edges of the territory, where the most isolated people lived, God gathers a people. The name reflects the faith that the Lord does not leave His most remote cities outside of His attention and blessing.
H6909.emploi: Kabtseel appears only three times in the Bible. It first appears in the list of cities in the Negev assigned to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:21), listed among the fortified cities of the south. It is then mentioned twice in connection with Benaja: this renowned warrior of David was from Kabtseel (2 Samuel 23:20) or originated from Kabtseel (1 Chronicles 11:22). These references show that even this small border town produced a prominent military leader in the service of the king.
H6909.portee: This place teaches us that God's providence extends to the most distant and seemingly poorest places. Benaja, born in this desert and isolated city, became one of David's three chief warriors — proof that God deserves no less trust in remote places than in centers of power. It is an invitation to see the forgotten corners of the world as fields of divine blessing.

sens: Action of bringing together
Group of people or things gathered
Forced gathering, coercive assembly
H6910.detail:
1. The word refers to the action of bringing together dispersed people or things. It is the active process of gathering: taking what is scattered and placing it in one location. In Ezekiel 22:20, God speaks of gathering His people as one gathers metals in a crucible before melting them — an image of judgment and purification.

2. The word can also refer to the group itself, the people or things once gathered. It is the result of the gathering: a unified whole in one place.

3. In the context of Ezekiel, this gathering takes on a tone of constraint and judgment. It is not a simple convocation: it is a gathering in anger and fury, where the people are treated like metal placed in fire to be purified by destruction.
H6910.origine: The word comes from the root קבץ (qabas), which means "to assemble" or "to gather." This root evokes the idea of taking scattered things and bringing them together in one point. It is very common in biblical Hebrew to express gathering, whether peaceful or violent.
H6910.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 22:20. In this passage, the prophet uses the image of gathering to announce God's judgment on Jerusalem. The inhabitants will be "gathered" in the city like metal in a crucible, then melted by the fire of divine anger. It is a gathering of judgment, not of salvation: it evokes the idea that God concentrates His people to purify them through trial.
H6910.portee: This word reminds us that the gathering ordered by God is not always an immediate blessing: it can be a judgment. For the Christian, this invites reflection on how God gathers His people — sometimes to protect them, sometimes to purify them through trial. It is also an image of the unity of God's people, even if that unity comes through trials.

sens: priestly city in ancient Israel
H6911.detail: Kibtsaïm is a Levitical city assigned to the sons of Kohath, a branch of the Levites responsible for the service of the sanctuary. It was located in the hill country of Ephraim, in the heart of the territory of the tribe of Ephraim. Joshua 21:22 mentions it among the forty-eight cities distributed to the Levites so that they would have places to live and pasture, according to the order established by Moses and executed after the conquest of the land.
H6911.origine: The name Kibtsaïm, from the Hebrew קִבְצַיִם (qivtsayim), literally means "the two gatherings" or "the two gatherings." The Bible also mentions an alternative name for this same city: Jokmeam (יׇקְמְעָם), which is found in other Levitical lists. These two names refer to the same place, perhaps due to local dialects or different traditions.
H6911.emploi: Kibtsaïm appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 21:22. It is listed among the priestly cities assigned by lot to the descendants of Kohath. This enumeration follows the order of the division of the promised land and reflects the religious organization of ancient Israel, where the Levites – without their own territory – received cities distributed among the different tribes to carry out their cultic functions.

sens: To place a dead body in the ground, in a tomb, to leave it there permanently
To perform funeral rites, to bury the deceased with honor
To put in the ground, to inter (passive form)
H6912.detail:
1. To bury means to place a corpse in the ground or a sepulcher — it is the concrete and definitive act of depositing the dead. Genesis 50:7 describes Joseph going up to "bury" his father: it is to transport the body and place it in the tomb. What happens concretely is taking the dead and entrusting them to the burial.
2. To bury also means to perform the funeral rites with the respect due: to render to the deceased the honors and rituals appropriate to their status. Judges 16:31 reports that Samson's brothers "buried him" between Zorea and Eshtaol "in the tomb of Manoah, his father" — it is not only to inter the body, but to place it with dignity alongside the family.
3. In the passive form ("to be buried"), the word indicates what happens to the body: it now rests in the grave. Genesis 15:15 promises the patriarch: "You shall be buried in a good old age" — a blessing formula that expresses a peaceful death, followed by an honorable burial.
H6912.origine: The Hebrew verb קָבַר (qavar) evokes the fundamental image of burying, hiding. Its root expresses the act of covering, putting away under the ground. The word is also used for the burial itself (קֶבֶר, qéver, "tomb") and for the one who buries (קַבָּר, qabbār, "gravedigger"). It is an ancient and concrete verb that refers to a universal act: the burial of one who has left life.
H6912.emploi: The verb appears more than 120 times in the Old Testament, especially in Genesis, where it accompanies the long patriarchal genealogies: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and their wives are buried in family tombs in Canaan. The act of burying is very important for the Hebrews: it is a filial duty and an act of respect towards ancestors. Kings are "buried" (2 Kings 14:20: "he was buried in Jerusalem with his fathers"), judges (Judges 10:2), prophets (1 Samuel 25:1). Sometimes the lack of burial is a curse (2 Kings 9:10 mentions Jezebel who will not be buried). The usage varies: one can bury with honor, or leave a dead person unburied — which is a disgrace. The verb can also take on the meaning of mass burial during disasters (Numbers 11:34, after God's judgment).
H6912.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that death is not oblivion: it is a solemn act that recognizes the dignity of the deceased and honors their memory. To bury with dignity is to confess that a life mattered. To refuse or neglect a burial is a profound indignity. In the background, one glimpses the Hebrew conviction that resting alongside one's fathers in the family tomb is a blessing, a peace granted to the one who departs.

sens: A hole dug in the ground to place a dead body
Cave or constructed space designed to receive the dead
Place of burial and final rest
In a figurative sense, destruction or annihilation
H6913.detail:
1. The tomb is primarily a hole, an excavation made in the soil or rock to receive a corpse and keep it from view. When Abraham asks Heth for a tomb (Genesis 23:4), he is simply seeking a place to bury his wife Sarah, away from the living.
2. The tomb can also be a more solid and durable construction or cave, intended to hold the remains of several generations of the same family. Thus Gideon is buried in the tomb of his father Joash (Judges 8:32), as an act of familial piety and continuity.
3. More broadly, the tomb refers to the final resting place of one who dies, the spot where their remains lie. When Job expresses a wish to go directly from the womb to the tomb (Job 10:19), he conveys the idea that the tomb is the inevitable destination of all human life.
4. In a rarer and poetic usage, the word takes on a figurative sense of destruction or ruin: the weapons of the warrior are compared to an open tomb (Jeremiah 5:16), an image of death and desolation.
H6913.origine: The Hebrew word qèver comes from a root meaning "to dig" or "to excavate." It is a very ancient and common word used to denote the dug space or pit where the dead are buried. In the Hebrew Bible, it appears 67 times and always refers to a physical or symbolic reality related to death and burial. The Greek of the Old Testament Septuagint translates it as mnêma or taphos.
H6913.emploi: The tomb appears 62 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in historical accounts and wisdom literature. For Abraham and his descendants (Genesis), it is the family property that is acquired and passed down from generation to generation. Among the kings of Israel (2 Kings, 2 Chronicles), the royal tomb becomes the place of their legitimacy and honor: being buried in the tombs of the kings is a mark of nobility, while being excluded from them (like Ahaz in 2 Chronicles 28:27) is a disgrace. In Job and the Psalms, the tomb becomes an image of mortal condition and nothingness. The word even acquires a figurative charge among the prophets (Jeremiah 5:16) to evoke ruin.
H6913.portee: The tomb reminds the believer that every human being, from the most powerful king to the humblest peasant, shares the same destiny: death and return to the earth. It is an invitation to live soberly, to seek what lasts beyond the grave, and to value the dignity of burial, as it recognizes the humanity of the one who dies. For the Christian, the empty tomb of Christ (resurrection) transforms the meaning of the grave: it is no longer the final term, but a surpassed stage.

sens: Station of Israel in the desert, three encampments after Sinai
Place where the people were buried for yielding to desire
Location that recalls divine judgment on carnal desires
H6914.detail: 1. Kibroth-Hattaava is a stop in Israel's journey through the desert, located three encampments from Sinai toward the Gulf of Aqaba. It is a resting place mentioned in the itinerary of the people during the Exodus (Numbers 33:16-17). 2. This site received its infamous name because the people were buried there after rebelling against God: the Israelites demanded meat with groans of desire, dissatisfied with the manna, and the Lord sent quail. But while they devoured the meat, a plague struck them (Numbers 11:34). 3. The name itself—"Graves of Desire"—carries a spiritual message: it commemorates God's judgment on those who, freed from Egypt and miraculously fed, despised divine provision to satisfy their fleshly desires. Paul cites it to warn the Corinthians not to crave evil as they did (1 Corinthians 10:6).
H6914.origine: The Hebrew name literally means "graves" (qibrôt) "of desire" (taʿăwâh). It evokes the image of a cemetery leaving its traces in the desert, named to forever remind of the breach of covenant: not a beautiful site or a simple crossroads, but a grave that cries out the name of the sin that filled it. This name has educational and memorial value in the biblical narrative.
H6914.emploi: Kibroth-Hattaava appears five times in Scripture: in Numbers 11, in the immediate account of the people's rebellion and punishment; then in Numbers 33, in the complete list of desert stops, where it is named twice as a starting and ending point; finally in Deuteronomy 9:22, where Moses reminds the people, to the next generation, of the three places where they angered the Lord: Taberah, Massah, and Kibroth-Hattaava. At each occurrence, the place embodies a lesson of sacred history, a warning against desire and unfaithfulness.
H6914.portee: This place serves as an educational sign in Scripture: its name carries the memory of judgment. For the believer, Kibroth-Hattaava reminds that God does not abandon His people to their desires, but can chastise those who despise His provision and kindness. It is a warning against carnal rebellions and a call to gratitude for divine faithfulness, even in the desert of present life.

sens: To bend the head and upper body downwards, as a sign of respect or submission
To prostrate oneself, to throw oneself to the ground before someone
To express through this gesture one's adherence, respect, or worship
H6915.detail:
1. The word primarily describes the physical gesture: lowering the head and leaning the body forward. This is what the man does before Abraham in Genesis 24:26 when he "bowed and prostrated himself" in recognition of God's intervention. The gesture is often accompanied by a more complete prostration, where one throws oneself to the ground.

2. The gesture signifies submission or homage rendered to someone greater: Jacob's sons "bowed and prostrated themselves" before their father in Genesis 43:28, thus acknowledging his authority. Balaam in Numbers 22:31 "bowed and prostrated himself on his face" before the angel of the Lord, accepting the divine command. Bathsheba in 1 Kings 1:31 "bowed her face to the ground" before King David, marking her respect.

3. But above all, to bow expresses religious worship and the heart's adherence to what God does. The people in Exodus 12:27 "bowed and prostrated themselves" upon learning of the salvation wrought by God at Passover. The assembly in Nehemiah 8:6 "bowed and prostrated themselves before the Lord" while listening to the Law read publicly. The bodily gesture expresses obedience and reverence of the heart.
H6915.origine: The Hebrew verb קדד (qadad) has as its root image the head that inclines or bends. It is related to other Hebrew words describing movements of bending or curving the body. The verb always appears in the Qal (simple form) and is regularly accompanied by the verb "to prostrate" (שׁחה, shaha), which shows that bowing is often the first movement of a deeper genuflection.
H6915.emploi: The verb קדד appears 15 times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively to describe the bowing of respect or worship before God, a king, or a figure of authority. The most frequent examples are found in the historical books (Genesis, Exodus, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and in the account of the reading of the Law in Nehemiah. The verb is always a conscious and voluntary act: it is a gesture that the subject chooses to perform. It often appears at key moments where one recognizes the presence, power, or divine authority. Almost every time, it is associated with a prostration (another verb or even construction), as if the bowing initiates the more complete act of worship.
H6915.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds that true worship engages both body and spirit: to bow one's head is to acknowledge with one's whole being the majesty of the one before whom one stands. The human gesture of bowing is the visible and honest expression of what is happening in the heart. It also illuminates the dignity conferred upon those before whom one bows, whether they are representatives of God or bearers of His authority. Finally, this voluntary act of reverence calls the Christian to cultivate an inner attitude of humility and submission to God.

sens: Aromatic spice derived from the bark of a tropical tree
Precious ingredient of the perfume used in the worship of the tabernacle
H6916.detail:
1. Cassia is a fragrant spice obtained from the bark of a tropical tree related to cinnamon. It emits a warm and pleasant aroma, highly sought after in antiquity. In Exodus 30:24, it is part of the composition of the sacred perfume intended for the tabernacle, alongside other rare and costly ingredients: it is a luxury reserved for the worship of God.
2. As a commercial commodity, cassia was a valuable good, traded along the trade routes of the ancient East. In Ezekiel 27:19, it is listed among the exchange items brought to the markets of Tyre, a prosperous city, revealing its economic importance and rarity in the Mediterranean world.
H6916.origine: The Hebrew word qiddah refers to the fragrant bark of a tropical tree, probably identical or very close to cinnamon. Its precise origin is lost in the ancient history of trade between the Middle East and tropical regions of Asia. In Greek, this word is translated as "cassia" (κασία), a term that has traveled into European languages to designate this spice.
H6916.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. First in Exodus 30:24, where it is included in the recipe for the sacred perfume of the tabernacle — a royal composition intrinsically linked to the worship rendered to God. Then in Ezekiel 27:19, in a list of the commercial riches of Tyre: cassia symbolizes the treasures of the distant East, these precious goods that fuel international trade and the luxury of prosperous cities. In both cases, it is a rare and costly substance.
H6916.portee: For the Christian, cassia in the worship of the tabernacle reminds us that God delights in what is beautiful, fragrant, and precious. The use of rare spices in divine service shows that the best materials and the finest aromas deserve to be offered to Him. It invites us to see worship as an act of generosity and respect, where nothing is too good to honor His presence.

sens: Very ancient time, distant, going back to the distant past
H6917.detail: 1. The word designates a time very far removed from that of the speaker, a distant past. In the Song of Deborah, Deborah refers to the torrent of Kishon that engulfed the enemies of Israel: she calls it the torrent of "ancient times" to emphasize that what she celebrates is part of a long history, that God's acts for His people do not date from yesterday (Judges 5:21).
H6917.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of what precedes, what goes forward — hence the meaning of "what has gone forward," that is, the past, the ancient. It is a poetic way of speaking about the depth of time.
H6917.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the Song of Deborah (Judges 5), which is one of the oldest poems in the Old Testament. The context is a war celebration: Deborah and Barak sing of the victory that Israel has won over Sisera's army. The expression "torrent of ancient times" solemnly enhances the event by placing it in the continuity of sacred history.
H6917.portee: This word invites us to see each intervention of God in the present history as the echo of a plan that extends far beyond our immediate view. Recognizing that God acts "from ancient times" strengthens faith in His faithfulness and constancy.

sens: Separated, set apart for God, distinct from the profane
Pure, without stain, without guilt
Worthy of reverence and worship, awe-inspiring
Dedicated to the worship and service of God
Belonging to God and bearing His mark
H6918G.detail:
1. The word first evokes separation: what is holy is set apart, different from the rest, reserved for God alone. Exodus 19:6 shows this well: Israel becomes "a holy nation," that is, chosen and distinguished among the peoples to serve God. It is a visible boundary between what belongs to God and what belongs to the ordinary world.
2. Holiness also means moral and spiritual purity: absence of guilt, evil, or what defiles. Leviticus 19:2 states clearly: "You shall be holy, for I am holy." It is a call to inner purification, to reject evil as one rejects filth.
3. The holy inspires a respectful fear: it is what is awe-inspiring, majestic, that inspires worship. Psalms 99:3 expresses this: "Let them praise your great and awesome name! He is holy!" The holiness of God makes humans aware of His greatness.
4. Practically, holy designates what is consecrated to religious worship: priests, offerings, places of the sanctuary are "holy" because they are reserved for God. Leviticus 24:9 speaks of the "most holy" bread that belongs to the service of the temple.
5. At the deepest level, holiness is the very essence of God. When He is called "the Holy One of Israel" (Isaiah 17:7, Isaiah 43:14), it is not just a title, but the revelation that God is radically separate, pure, perfect, and incomparable.
H6918G.origine: The Hebrew word קָדוֹשׁ (qadosh) comes from a root meaning "to cut, to separate." This image of separation is at the heart of the meaning: the holy is what is cut off from the rest, set apart. Throughout the Old Testament, words of the same family (like קֹדֶשׁ, "holiness" or "sanctuary") share this idea of distinction. Holiness first describes the action of God who separates, then the state of what is thus separated for Him. That is why God Himself is called "the Holy One": He is absolutely separate from creation, without mixture with it.
H6918G.emploi: The word appears 99 times in the Bible, particularly in Leviticus and Psalms. It is applied to God, first and foremost ("the Holy One of Israel"), but also to priests (Leviticus 21:6-8), offerings (Leviticus 6:9), days (Exodus 19:6), and everything consecrated to worship. Israel itself is called "a holy nation" (Exodus 19:6, Deuteronomy 7:6), not because it is virtuous, but because it has been chosen and separated. The word is also used as a moral command: "Be holy, for I am holy" (Leviticus 11:44-45) means that believers must imitate the holiness of God by separating themselves from sin. Thus, the meaning oscillates between an objective reality (what is reserved for God) and an existential call (to become pure and separated from evil).
H6918G.portee: For the Christian, holiness is not an abstract notion but a concrete call to separation from evil and imitation of God. This word reveals that God is fundamentally other, incomparable, and that He wants those who serve Him to resemble Him. To be holy is not to achieve absolute perfection, but to be voluntarily set apart for God, rejecting what defiles. It is an invitation to take seriously the belonging to God and to live in accordance with this reality.

sens: Separated, set apart for God
Belonging to God, consecrated
A pious person who fears God
Pure, without moral blemish
H6918H.detail:
1. The word "holy" primarily designates what is separated from the common, reserved for God. When Moses tests the Levites (Numbers 16:7), the one whom the Lord chooses will be recognized as holy, that is, marked and consecrated by God for a particular service.

2. A saint is a person who belongs to God and lives under His lordship. The saints of Psalm 34:10 are those who fear the Lord; by fearing Him and remaining faithful, they enter into a relationship of consecration with Him. Aaron is called "the holy one of the Lord" (Psalms 106:16) because he was chosen and set apart for divine service.

3. A saint is also a pious man, someone virtuous who walks with God. The woman in 2 Kings 4:9 recognizes that the man who regularly visits her house is a "holy man of God": she sees in him someone consecrated, trustworthy, who lives in communion with God.

4. Holiness also implies moral purity and the absence of guilt. The one who is holy has turned away from evil to turn towards God and seeks to remain pure in the eyes of the Lord.
H6918H.origine: The word "holy" comes from a Hebrew root that means "to separate" or "to set apart." It evokes the image of something withdrawn from common use, reserved solely for sacred use. Holiness is therefore not primarily an abstract moral quality: it is a concrete separation, an exclusive belonging to God. Related words designate the sanctuary, worship, and consecration.
H6918H.emploi: The word "holy" appears 7 times in the provided passages, always to describe people or things marked by their connection to God. It applies to Aaron, priest of the Lord; to the faithful who fear the Lord (Psalms 34:10; Deuteronomy 33:3); to a man of God recognized for his piety (2 Kings 4:9). It is a term that values the one to whom it is applied: to be holy is to be recognized as belonging to God and living according to His will. The context shows that holiness results from God's choice (Numbers 16:7) and is expressed in the fear of the Lord and faithfulness.
H6918H.portee: Understanding that saints are primarily people set apart for God helps the Christian grasp the call to consecration. To be holy is not an unattainable moral perfection, but a response to God's election: it is to give oneself to Him, to obey Him, and to walk with Him. It is also an invitation to recognize the saints among us, those whose fear of God and faithfulness distinguish them in the community of faith.

sens: To set fire to something, to ignite a flame
To catch fire, to ignite
To trigger, to set in motion (figuratively)
H6919.detail:
1. To light a fire or a torch: it is the concrete action of bringing forth the flame. In Isaiah 50:11, the people who "light a fire" and carry torches seek to illuminate their path, but God warns them that they will suffer the consequences.
2. To ignite, to catch fire: the fire itself ignites and spreads. In Isaiah 64:1, it is like a fire that ignites in dry wood and quickly consumes, an image of strength and swiftness.
3. To trigger God's anger, to make it burst forth: this is the figurative use, very frequent in our verses. God's anger "ignites" (Deuteronomy 32:22, Jeremiah 15:14), or the people "light" divine anger through their unfaithfulness (Jeremiah 17:4). It is a powerful image: anger bursts forth suddenly and spreads like an uncontrollable fire.
H6919.origine: The Hebrew root expresses the idea of making something burst forth, to ignite. The verb describes the lively and sudden action of setting fire or igniting. It is a concrete word at its core, which then applies to all acts or feelings that "burst forth" or "explode" suddenly.
H6919.emploi: This verb appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always in connection with fire or anger. Four times, it is God's anger that "ignites": it burns to the foundations of the abode of the dead (Deuteronomy 32:22), or it is provoked by the people's unfaithfulness (Jeremiah 15:14, 17:4). Once, it is men who "light" a fire in the literal sense (Isaiah 50:11). The spiritual use predominates: the verb serves to describe how divine anger bursts forth and spreads like a wildfire in the face of disobedience.
H6919.portee: This word reminds the reader of the reality and power of God's anger: it is not an abstraction, but something that "ignites" and burns, that consumes. It is a serious warning: our acts of unfaithfulness are never without consequence. But it is also an invitation to respectful fear of God and obedience, so that this anger does not consume us.

sens: Feverish illness characterized by an abnormal elevation of body temperature
Affliction sent by God as punishment for the unfaithful
H6920.detail:
1. Fever is an illness that causes a high body temperature and weakens the sufferer. It makes the eyes languid (Leviticus 26:16) and progressively consumes the sick person.
2. In the curses of Deuteronomy and Leviticus, fever is not just a simple natural misfortune: it is a direct blow from God striking His unfaithful people. It ranks among the fearsome plagues—consumption, inflammation, burning heat—that the Lord sends to punish the abandonment of His covenant (Deuteronomy 28:22).
H6920.origine: The Hebrew word qaddachat comes from a root that evokes intense heat and burning. Its image is that of a heat that consumes and progressively weakens. Biblical texts always place it among serious illnesses, never as a minor ailment.
H6920.emploi: The word appears twice in Israel, exclusively in the passages of covenantal curses from Deuteronomy and Leviticus. In Leviticus 26:16, it accompanies terror and consumption to weaken the one who transgresses the covenant. In Deuteronomy 28:22, it is part of a systematic enumeration of various plagues (inflammation, burning heat, desiccation) that God sends in cascade against the unfaithful. The usage is therefore theological and legal: fever symbolizes divine sanction, it is never recounted as a simple common illness.
H6920.portee: For the biblical reader, fever reminds us that the violation of the covenant with God is not without consequence: God defends His people by disciplining them. It is not a promise of illness, but a solemn warning of the spiritual cost of unfaithfulness. It invites us to take seriously our commitment to God and to recognize that our well-being depends on our obedience.

sens: The direction of the rising sun
The wind that blows from this direction, often destructive and scorching
What relates to the direction of the east, which is located towards the east
H6921.detail:
1. The east is the geographical direction of the east, the side of the world where the sun rises. It is primarily a landmark in space: in Ezekiel 43:2, "the glory of the God of Israel was coming from the east" means that the divine manifestation was coming from the side of the east, from the rising sun. It is a concrete direction that the Bible uses to locate places and draw boundaries, as in Ezekiel 47:18 where "the eastern side will be the Jordan." 
2. The east also refers to the east wind, this hot and dry breath that comes from the desert. In Genesis 41:6, Pharaoh sees "seven thin ears scorched by the east wind" — this wind destroys the crops. It is a wind of destruction and drought: in Ezekiel 17:10, the plant "will wither when the east wind strikes it." This wind often symbolizes divine judgment in the Bible. 
3. The adjective "eastern" qualifies anything that is turned towards the east or that comes from the east. In Ezekiel 40:23, we measure "the eastern gate" of the temple: it is the gate that opens to the east side. This purely directional meaning applies to buildings, gates, and boundaries.
H6921.origine: The Hebrew word קָדִים (qadim) comes from the root קדם (qedem), which means "east" and also "formerly, the past." This root reflects an ancient way of thinking: the east is the side of the "front," as one would envision the east in front of oneself (hence "past" as well, since the east is where the new day comes). The word can take on a figurative sense of destruction and judgment when it refers to the east wind, which brings drought to the east.
H6921.emploi: The word appears 64 times in the Bible, especially in Ezekiel (over 40 occurrences), notably in the detailed description of the future temple in chapters 40-48. In the texts of Moses (Exodus 10:13, 14:21), the east wind is an instrument of divine judgment against Egypt: it is by this wind that the plagues manifest. In Genesis 41, the east wind scorches the ears and represents the judgment of the seven years of famine. In the prophets (Jeremiah, Hosea, Ezekiel), it often symbolizes punishment: in Isaiah 27:8, God "punishes by exile, taking them away by the fierce breath of the east wind." In Ezekiel 40-48, the word loses this symbolism of destruction and becomes a simple geographical designation: it is about measuring and describing the sides, gates, and dimensions of the restored temple.
H6921.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God uses creation — even natural phenomena like the wind — to execute His judgment. But it also shows that direction, space, and material order matter: Ezekiel's vision of the divine glory returning from the east (43:2) heralds renewal. This humble spatial term invites us to recognize that everything that exists, from geography to meteorology, is in God's hands.

sens: Separated, consecrated to God, free from defilement
Celestial being, angel, or spiritual being belonging to the divine court
Member of the people of God, faithful believer destined to share in divine glory
H6922.detail: 1. The word primarily describes what is separated from the profane and consecrated to God, pure and sacred. In Daniel 4:8, we speak of "the spirit of the holy gods" — a power that emanates from the divine sphere and opposes the impure world of men. 2. It also designates celestial beings, angels, or spiritual creatures that surround the throne of God. In Daniel 4:13, "one of those who watch and are holy" is a celestial being descended from heaven, a divine messenger. 3. By extension, it applies to the faithful of the Most High, those who belong to God and participate in His eternal glory. In Daniel 7:18 and 7:25, "the saints of the Most High" are the people of God who will receive the eternal kingdom and against whom the horn (hostile power) will wage war.
H6922.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to cut," "to separate." A holy person is therefore someone or something that is separated, set apart from the rest. This is the central idea: holiness is the state of one who belongs to God and is radically distinct from others. The word is very common in the sacred texts of Mesopotamia and the Near East to designate what pertains to the gods.
H6922.emploi: This word appears 12 times in biblical Aramaic, exclusively in the book of Daniel (chapters 4, 5, and 7). In the early usages (Daniel 4:8-18), it qualifies the divine spirit that resides in Daniel, the one who gives him supernatural wisdom and understanding. From Daniel 7 onward, the term gradually changes in meaning: it no longer designates an impersonal power but the "saints of the Most High," the people of God themselves. In Daniel 7:21-25, these saints suffer persecution from a hostile power (the little horn), but they ultimately receive the eternal kingdom. The word thus takes on a collective and eschatological dimension: it speaks of the glorious future of the faithful people.
H6922.portee: For the believer, this word reveals that holiness is not primarily a moral quality, but a belonging: to be holy is to be separated for God, pure from everything that diverts one from Him. Daniel receives in him "the spirit of the holy gods" and becomes an instrument of wisdom. The saints of the Most High, persecuted in the world, have a guaranteed destiny: they will reign with God for eternity. It is a promise of final victory that sustains faith in trials.

sens: To stand in front of someone or something to confront or welcome them
To meet someone in order to receive them with hospitality
To anticipate, to precede: to happen before, earlier than expected
To accompany forward, to guide the way
To intervene to stop, to block
To manifest to someone, to appear to them
H6923.detail:
1. To go before someone primarily means to meet them face to face, to stand in front of them to confront (Psalms 17:13: "Arise, O Lord! Confront him, bring him low"). It is a position of opposition or direct confrontation.

2. In a friendly context, it means to go to meet someone to receive them, as one goes out to welcome an important guest. In Deuteronomy 23:4, Moab did not want to "go before" Israel with bread and water: to refuse to go before is to refuse hospitality.

3. To anticipate or precede means to arrive before something happens, to foresee it. In Job 30:27, calamity "surprises" (precedes) him: it comes upon him before he expects it. In Psalms 88:14, the prayer "rises" in the morning, preceding the day.

4. To go before someone can also mean to precede them on the way, to guide or lead them forward (an image of a leader walking ahead of their people).

5. In 2 Kings 19:32, the Lord says that the king of Assyria will not "present" shields against Jerusalem: it is to intervene to block, to oppose his action.

6. In the Psalms (59:11; 89:15), God "goes before" the psalmist or his faithful ones "come to meet you": the divine presence manifests, it moves towards humanity.
H6923.origine: The Hebrew verb qadam means properly "to go forward", "to walk before". Its root evokes the idea of precedence, of an earlier position in space or time. The noun qdm (in Hebrew) means "formerly, in ancient times": hence the image of a past that "precedes" us. The noun qedem designates the east, the direction of the rising sun and of beginnings. Thus, the verb unites two ideas: that of physical position (to stand in front) and that of temporal priority (to precede, to anticipate).
H6923.emploi: This verb appears 25 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the Piel forms ("to come to meet") and Hiphil ("to bring before"). The usages cover three areas: welcome or hospitality (Deuteronomy 23:4: not coming to meet someone is to reject them), confrontation or divine help (Psalms 17:13; 18:6; 59:11: the Lord goes before his faithful to defend them), and anticipation or prevention (Job 30:27: calamity surprises him). The meaning nuances according to the subject: it is an act of friendship when it is a human, an act of power when it is God. Especially in the Psalms, God "goes before" those who seek him, marking his active goodwill.
H6923.portee: This word teaches that God does not wait passively: he comes to meet those who seek and plead with him. He anticipates, he precedes our needs, he intervenes to protect us. For the believer, "going before" someone is an act of honor and hospitality; refusing to do so (Deuteronomy 23:4) is a haughty rejection. Finally, this verb shows that God is always the one who acts first: he comes to meet us long before we are able to go to meet him.

sens: Geographical direction of the east, where the sun rises
Nomadic peoples living east of Israel
Ancient times, distant past
H6924A.detail:
1. The word designates the direction of the east, defined by the rising sun. It is the fundamental direction in biblical orientation: when speaking of a place "to the east", it indicates that it is towards the east. Ezekiel 25:4 uses it with precise geographical meaning.
2. By extension, "the sons of the East" (or "the people of the East") refers to the nomadic and Bedouin peoples living east of the Jordan and Israel, known for their caravans and camels. Judges 6:3 and 7:12 present them as invaders coming from the eastern desert with Midian and Amalek, their troops numbering in the thousands, with countless camels.
3. The word can also evoke antiquity or ancientness, the time before, what comes from the distant past — although this meaning is less developed in these usages.
H6924A.origine: The Hebrew word qédem comes from a root meaning "before, to advance". The east is what stands "before" one who looks towards the rising sun — the ancient reference direction in Semitic culture. This same root gives words in the family of ancient times and the past. The basic image is that of what precedes, hence the dual meaning: the east (direction of the rising sun) and antiquity (what comes from before).
H6924A.emploi: The word appears 6 times in these passages, all in military and geographical contexts. Judges 6 and 7 use it to refer to the Bedouin peoples of the eastern desert — Midian, Amalek, and their allies — who invade Israel like a plague of locusts. Judges 8:10 confirms this identification by speaking of the "entire army of the sons of the East" defeated by Gideon. Ezekiel 25 uses the expression to announce that the peoples of the east will conquer and inhabit the territory of Ammon. The word always remains in this collective and territorial sense: the peoples of a region, not just an abstract direction.
H6924A.portee: This word reminds us that for the Bible, the east often symbolizes what is foreign, powerful, and threatening — the place from which dangers come. It is from the eastern desert that nomads emerge with their countless camels. But it is also towards the east that God places Eden and from where he calls his prophets. Thus, the east is never neutral: it concentrates both the divine promise and the challenges of the world.

sens: The direction towards which the sun rises
From the side where the sun rises, speaking of a region or a geographical boundary
Speaking of an orientation or a face of a building or an object
H6924B.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the cardinal point east, where the sun rises. It is the fundamental direction, the one by which the day begins. In Genesis 13:14, Abram is commanded to look towards the east among the four directions.

2. It applies to regions, lands, or peoples located towards the east. Numbers 34:3 and 34:15 define the boundaries of the Israelites' territory "on the eastern side": it refers to the lands beyond the Jordan, towards the east. Joshua 18:20 mentions "the eastern side" of the Jordan as a natural boundary.

3. It also designates the orientation of a face, a façade, or a side of a religious building. Exodus 27:13 and Leviticus 16:14 describe elements of the sanctuary "on the eastern side": the courtyard and the mercy seat had a face turned towards the east, a direction considered paramount.
H6924B.origine: The Hebrew word קֵדֶם (qèdem) comes from a root that expresses the idea of what is "before" or "ancient". The east is indeed "before" one who turns according to the course of the sun, and it is the direction of the day that begins, thus of the first time. This root is the basis of other Hebrew words expressing ancientness or anteriority. In Greek, the word is translated as ἀνατολή (anatolè), literally "rising" of the sun.
H6924B.emploi: The word appears about 25 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the legislative and narrative books. It is very frequent in geographical and architectural descriptions: delimitation of the tribes' territory (Numbers 34, Joshua 15 and 18), orientation of the sanctuary and its furnishings (Exodus 27, Leviticus 1 and 16), arrangement of the camp in the desert (Numbers 2 and 3). In these contexts, the east is not a poetic direction but a precise and constant reference of the holy organization of Israel. The word is sometimes translated as "eastern" when it qualifies a region or a boundary.
H6924B.portee: For the biblical reader, the east holds symbolic and practical importance: it is the side of light, of what unfolds before the day. The fact that the sanctuary, the camp, and the promised lands are systematically oriented towards the east suggests that this direction is favored in the order intended by God for his people. This invites the believer to recognize that God guides his people according to a wise and intended order, visible even in the orientation of space.

sens: the direction of the rising sun
the regions located to the east of a given land
antiquity, ancient times
that which is in front, ahead of someone or something
H6924G.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the geographical direction of east, the side where the sun rises. This is the most direct spatial meaning: "The Lord God planted a garden in Eden, toward the east" (Genesis 2:8). The borders of Israel are described in relation to the east: "it shall descend from Shepham to Riblah, on the east side of Ain" (Numbers 34:11).
2. The word then refers to the peoples and regions that inhabit the east: "the wisdom of Solomon surpassed the wisdom of all the sons of the East" (1 Kings 4:30) speaks of the eastern peoples renowned for their knowledge.
3. By temporal extension, it signifies antiquity and past times: the east also evokes "that which is ancient." The word can be translated as "formerly" or "from antiquity."
4. Finally, it can express the idea of "that which is in front" in a spatial or temporal sense: that which comes forward, that which precedes. It is the image of the depth of the past.
H6924G.origine: The Hebrew word קֶדֶם comes from an ancient root that evokes what is in front, before oneself. This root seems related to the idea of the face or the front. In ancient Hebrew, "the east" literally means "that which is in front," as one would visualize the east facing oneself when orienting. The word has derivatives that express antiquity: קִדְמָה (Qidma) also means "formerly." This evolution from spatial to temporal is characteristic of Hebrew thought: the east, the direction of the beginning of the day, also symbolizes the beginning of time.
H6924G.emploi: The word הופץ appears in the Hebrew Bible 21 times, mainly for geographical and chronological descriptions. In Genesis and the historical books, it serves to locate places: "As they journeyed from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar" (Genesis 11:2). In the prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel), it designates either eastern regions or, by context, antiquity. Job 1:3 uses it for the wealth of the patriarchs "of ancient times." The word can also have a moral nuance: in Isaiah, the "sons of the East" embody a human wisdom that does not replace divine revelation.
H6924G.portee: This word reminds the reader that biblical geography is never neutral: the east, the rising sun, is the biblical symbol of beginning, novelty, and new grace. Conversely, the antiquity embodied by this same word invites respect for the wisdom of the past and the ancient acts of God. For the believer, "the east" is also the horizon of expectation: it is from there that light comes, an image of Christ and His coming.

sens: Ancient, distant times that preceded the present
Historical past: earlier days, a bygone era
Direction of the east, the rising sun
Beginning, origins
Eternal past, limitless time
H6924H.detail:
1. The word designates the time that preceded the present moment, distant and bygone. This is what one thinks of when recalling ancient events: "I remember the days of old; I meditate on all Your works" (Psalms 143:5) — the psalmist looks back at God's acts in the past.

2. It evokes the ancient historical period, the time of the fathers and the vanished generations. The Psalms often speak of "the works You have done in their days, in the days of old" (Psalms 44:2), celebrating what God has done in past history.

3. The word can also indicate the direction of the east, the rising sun. This meaning arises from the image: the east is "in front of" one who looks north, hence "that which is in front" = the east.

4. It applies to the origins and the beginning of things, as when speaking of what has been from the start. Wisdom proclaims: "The Lord possessed me at the beginning of His work, before His works of old" (Proverbs 8:22-23), where "of old" refers to what comes from the beginning of time.

5. In a theological context, the word evokes the eternal past, that limitless time before creation. God speaks of His plans that He "resolved from of old" (Isaiah 37:26), expressing His knowledge and will that precede the ages.
H6924H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that primarily evokes the position "in front" — that which is ahead of oneself. From this spatial image arise the two major meanings: "the east" (the direction in front of us at sunrise) and "the past" (for in Hebrew as in French, "in front" for time means "before," the past being that which precedes us). The same root has given rise to the verb "to prevent" or "to go before." In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears very often, revealing the richness of this notion in biblical thought regarding the past and eternity.
H6924H.emploi: The word appears 32 times in the Old Testament. It is particularly frequent in the Psalms (about ten occurrences), where it expresses meditation on God's past acts: the faithful remember His ancient deliverances to draw courage and confidence. It is also found in Isaiah and Jeremiah, where it evokes God's ancient plan regarding the history of nations. In Lamentations, it designates the happy days before the ruin of Jerusalem, with a nostalgic tone: "Let us remember the days of our affliction and our misery" (Lamentations 5:21). The word can have nuances: sometimes it is simply temporal ("formerly"), sometimes it carries an emotional charge (memories, nostalgia), and sometimes it is theological (God's eternal plan).
H6924H.portee: For the reader, this word invites looking to the past not with sterile regret, but to discover God's faithfulness. The Psalms teach that remembering the acts accomplished "formerly" strengthens us in the face of present trials. It is also a word that opens the consciousness to eternity: God knows and masters the ancient time as well as the future, which solidifies faith in His sovereignty. At the same time, it reminds us that history has a direction — God does not act randomly, but according to a plan established since antiquity.

sens: Direction of the east, toward the rising sun
That which is in front of oneself, ahead
Ancient times, antiquity
The beginning of things
H6924I.detail:
1. The east designates the geographical direction of east, that of the rising sun — it is the cardinal point opposite to the west. In Job 23:8, Job seeks God by going to the east and then to the west, meaning he explores all horizons without finding Him.
2. The word also evokes that which is in front of oneself, ahead: the east is the direction that one looking east has "in front" of them, which can extend to any position of facade or front.
3. The east can signify the past, antiquity — that which was "before," at the beginning. It is the idea of yore, of former times, of that which belongs to the origins.
4. By extension, the word designates the very beginning of things, the starting point from which everything proceeds.
H6924I.origine: The Hebrew root suggests the idea of what is "in front" or "anterior." The word is related to roots that express movement forward or frontal position. The association between the east (orient) and antiquity comes from the same image: the east is in front of one who looks toward the morning horizon, and antiquity is "in front" of us in time — that which precedes us, which we see disappearing on the horizon of history.
H6924I.emploi: This word appears once in the Segond translations according to available data, in Job 23:8 where it designates the geographical east. Job seeks the face of God by traversing the four cardinal points: the east and the west, symbolizing an exhaustive and desperate quest. The word can also be used for antiquity or past times, although this dimension is not illustrated in this unique passage.
H6924I.portee: This verse reveals spiritual anguish: even in seeking God everywhere — across the earth and through time — one may feel abandoned. For the reader, it is a call to ask how they seek God: not merely through places or human efforts alone, but in the relationship of faith and in the word of God that manifests itself.

sens: In front of someone or something, in the space that separates them
In the presence of, under the gaze of
With the intention of, in service to
H6925.detail:
1. The word primarily describes a physical position: being placed in front of someone. In Ezra 4:18, a letter is read "in front of" the king — that is, under his eyes, in his direct presence. This spatial meaning is the most concrete.

2. It then means "in the presence of," in the sense of appearing before an authority or a court. In Daniel 3:13, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego are brought "in front of" the king: they appear with the purpose of giving an account or facing judgment. This is a moral and political space, not just physical.

3. The word can also express an intention or a service rendered: to act "in front of" someone means to act on their behalf or for their intention. In Daniel 2:18, Daniel's companions plead for mercy "on behalf of" the wise men, that is, in favor of a cause presented before God.
H6925.origine: This Aramaic word comes from a root meaning "before" or "in front of." It is related to Hebrew and Aramaic words of similar meaning. In biblical Aramaic, the preposition "in front of" always evokes a conscious, visible, current presence: not just a simple geometric space, but a relationship between the one who acts and the one in front of whom they act.
H6925.emploi: The word appears 38 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the books of Ezra and Daniel, which are written in Aramaic (or contain passages in Aramaic). It is used to describe actions that take place under the gaze of a king or authority: reading a letter, bringing someone to judgment, praying, worshiping. Its meaning varies little: it is always a relationship of visibility or dependence towards a presence. Sometimes it takes on an emotional nuance (fear, dread, in Daniel 6:26): the presence of the one before whom one stands inspires an emotion.
H6925.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us of the importance of acting "in front of" the Lord — that is, in awareness of His presence and gaze. It also evokes the notion of appearing, of giving an account, which resonates with the biblical idea of the final judgment and responsibility towards God. It is a humble preposition that places the user in a position of dependence or submission.

sens: Direction of the rising sun, cardinal point east
Region, country, or area located to the east of a reference point
H6926.detail:
1. The word first designates the geographical direction of the rising sun, the cardinal point east. This is the most concrete and direct meaning: we speak of the east as one would today. In Genesis 2:14, the Hiddekel flows "to the east of Assyria," that is, towards the east of that region.
2. By extension, it designates any region, territory, or area that is located to the east relative to a reference point. Thus, Cain settled "to the east of Eden" (Genesis 4:16), and the Philistines camped "to the east of Beth-Aven" (1 Samuel 13:5): in each case, a place is situated by indicating its position to the east of a known location.
H6926.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of going "before" or "forward." The east is thus the direction of forward, the one towards which one naturally advances — in ancient times, when one looked up in the morning, one would see the sun rising in front of oneself. This word is related to other Hebrew terms meaning "before," "face," or "anteriority." The image of the rising sun advancing in the sky gave rise to this term to designate the cardinal point east.
H6926.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the Segond, always to geographically locate a place in relation to the east. It is used mainly in foundational narratives (Genesis) and in military or prophetic descriptions (1 Samuel, Ezekiel). In each occurrence, it functions as a spatial marker: the east is a stable reference point for locating rivers, regions, or territories. The word remains constant in its geographical meaning, without figurative nuance.
H6926.portee: This word reminds the reader that the Bible speaks in terms of concrete spatial markers and real geography. Rivers flow, peoples camp, regions extend to the east or west: all of this is part of the story of a visible and ordered creation. For the believer, this invites recognition that God governs a real space, from the Garden of Eden to the lands of Gog.

sens: What was before, what preceded in time
The time or situation of the past
Something restored to its original state
H6927.detail:
1. The word first designates what preceded, what existed before a change. Thus in Ezekiel 36:11, God promises to restore Israel by saying "I want you to be inhabited as before": it is about returning to the previous state of prosperity.
2. It can also simply express anteriority in time, as in Psalms 129:6 where the grass must dry "before" it is pulled up, that is, before the moment of pulling up.
3. The word can also qualify a prestigious antiquity, the ancientness of a civilization. Isaiah 23:7 speaks of Tyre, whose "ancient origin" shows the past greatness of this joyful city.
H6927.origine: The Hebrew root fundamentally means "to go before, to precede." The word קַדְמָה (qadmah) thus designates what comes forward, what is from before — hence the idea of what precedes in time. This same root has generated other words related to "before," to "east" (the direction of the front) and to "antiquity." Aramaic uses the same word with the meaning "previously."
H6927.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Ezekiel and in the Psalms. It primarily expresses the idea of restoration: returning to the former state, to what was before a ruin or a fall (Ezekiel 16:55 repeats it three times for Sodom, Samaria, and Jerusalem). It can also simply mark temporal anteriority (Psalms 129:6) or qualify the past greatness of a city (Isaiah 23:7). Its use is always linked to a contrast between a more favorable past time and the present situation.
H6927.portee: This word teaches a comforting truth for the people of God: restoration and forgiveness are possible. When God promises to bring Israel back to its "former state," He shows that evil and ruin are not eternal, and that His grace can repair what has been broken. It is a word of hope for those who know the fall.

sens: As before, in the same manner as before
Previous state or situation
H6928.detail:
1. The word designates the habit or repeated practice that one had in the past. In Daniel 6:10, Daniel prays three times a day "previously": this means that he continues exactly as he did before, without changing his habit, even when the king has forbidden prayer.
