It conveys the idea of continuity, of faithful repetition of what was already done.
2. The word can also evoke the state or situation that existed before a change or event. It looks back to the past to show the contrast with the present, or to affirm that one is returning to what was.
H6928.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the same root as the Hebrew qad.mah (קַדְמָה), which means "to form" or "anterior." The root evokes the idea of what is "before" or "ancient," what comes from before. It is an adverb or adjective expressing priority in time.
H6928.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in Aramaic texts: in Ezra 5:11 and Daniel 6:10. In these two passages, it describes an action or a past situation to which one refers to emphasize continuity or return to the old habit. In Daniel 6:10, notably, "previously" (qad.mah) underscores Daniel's determination to pray as he always has, despite the king's prohibition.
H6928.portee: This word shows us how faithful believers like Daniel remain steadfast in their convictions and spiritual practices despite external pressures. The refusal to change "previously," that is, the continuity with one's prayer habits, expresses an unwavering fidelity to God — a powerful lesson to remain firm in faith even in the face of opposition.

sens: Son of Ishmael, ancestor of an Arab tribe
H6929.detail: 1. Kédma is a biblical character mentioned twice: he is the youngest son of Ishmael, himself the son of Abraham (Genesis 25:15). His name, which means "original" or "first," designates him among the twelve sons of Ishmael. He also appears in the account of 1 Chronicles 1:31, where he is listed with his brothers as sons of Ishmael, confirming his place in the genealogy of ancient Arab peoples.
H6929.origine: The name Kédma comes from Hebrew and literally means "original" or "the one who comes first." It designates one of the ancestors of the nomadic Arab peoples of the patriarchal era. In 1 Chronicles 5:19, he is also called Nodab, which shows that under different names, this son of Ishmael is recognized as the ancestor of a historically attested Arab tribe.
H6929.emploi: Kédma is mentioned twice in the Bible, both times in genealogical lists. First in Genesis 25:15, where he appears among the twelve sons of Ishmael listed after Abraham's death. Then in 1 Chronicles 1:31, which reiterates this same genealogy to establish the continuity of the peoples descended from Ishmael. These two passages place Kédma in the context of ancient Arab peoples, descendants of Ishmael, and show his importance in the genealogical tree of ancient Near Eastern nations.

sens: Located in the east, the direction where the sun rises
Coming from the east or concerning this direction
H6930.detail:
1. The word designates what belongs to the east, the direction of the rising sun. In Ezekiel 47:8, the miraculous waters that flow from the temple go toward the "eastern district" — that is, toward the Judean desert and the Jordan Valley that extend east of Jerusalem.
2. The word can also qualify what comes from the east or characterizes this region. It is a sacred geography: the east, in the Bible, is the direction of the rising sun and the Garden of Eden, imbued with spiritual meaning.
H6930.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to go before" or "to precede" — for the east is the point from which the day "precedes" the night, the place from which light comes. The same word can also denote "antiquity" or what is "from long ago": the east is primarily where time begins, where the day starts. The family includes other forms related to "before" and "precedence."
H6930.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 47:8, in the vision of the new Jerusalem and the sacred river that flows from it. The prophetic context shows its importance: the pure waters of the temple flowing toward the east symbolize the healing of the world and the expansion of salvation from the sanctuary in all directions — and particularly toward the east, the most distant and arid region. It is a rare but very rich word in the biblical geography of hope.
H6930.portee: This term invites the reader to meditate on the sacred directions in the biblical vision of the world. The east is never neutral in Scripture: it is where the sun rises, where the Lord comes from, where new life springs forth. By seeing the waters of the temple flow toward the east, one understands that the salvation brought by God is not reserved for the near: it extends to distant and hostile lands, to the ends of the earth.

sens: Related to the east, the direction of the rising sun
Coming from the east
Ancient, from long ago
Previous generation, ancestors
H6931G.detail:
1. The adjective primarily designates what belongs to the east, the direction of the rising sun. In Ezekiel 11:1, the "eastern gate" of the house of the Lord is the one facing east, toward the rising sun. Similarly, the "eastern sea" (Zechariah 14:8) is the one that extends toward the east, probably the Dead Sea.

2. The word can also qualify what comes from or emanates from the east. In Joel 2:20, the vanguard of the enemy from the north rushes into the "eastern sea," meaning it heads toward the east.

3. By a natural extension, "eastern" takes on the meaning of "ancient" or "from long ago," for what comes from the east is also what precedes, what has already occurred. It is the image of time advancing like the sun, and what is "eastern" is what has already taken place.

4. Applied to generations, the word designates past generations, ancestors. In Job 18:20, the "generations" or "previous generations" will be astonished at the ruin of the wicked: these are those who lived before.
H6931G.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root "qedem" (קֶדֶם), which primarily means "before" in time, then "east" in space — for in Hebrew, one locates oneself by looking east, from where light comes and where the day begins. From the same family, we find "qadmoni" (ancient, eastern) and related words that always describe what is in front, what precedes, whether in space (the east) or in time (the ancient).
H6931G.emploi: This word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the prophecies of Ezekiel and Zechariah, where it qualifies specific geographical directions: gates, sides, and bodies of water facing east. It always serves to describe the orientation of the territory of Israel and its temple. Only one occurrence (Job 18:20) uses the word in a temporal sense, to designate the generations that preceded. The transition from a spatial meaning to a temporal meaning reflects ancient Hebrew thought, where time and space are linked by the image of the sun rising in the east and progressing in the sky.
H6931G.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that the geography of God's people is not insignificant: the temple, the directions, the borders of the promised land have importance in God's plan. Recognizing the "east" in biblical texts helps visualize prophetic visions and understand how the Old Testament anchors divine word in a real and concrete territory.

sens: What belongs to a past time, distant
What has preceded and no longer exists
What occurred long ago
H6931H.detail: 1. The word designates what dates back to a bygone era, distant in time. It conveys the idea of antiquity, of what has depth. David refers to an "ancient" proverb to speak of wisdom known for a long time (1 Samuel 24:14): he draws from a source of teaching from the past. 2. It can evoke something that has disappeared or changed: God invites Israel not to remember the "former events" and what is "ancient," meaning to forget the misfortunes of old to welcome a new reality (Isaiah 43:18). 3. It also applies to words or acts that occurred long before the moment of the narrative. When God says: "Is it you of whom I spoke long ago by my servants the prophets?" he refers to predictions made long ago (Ezekiel 38:17). 4. The word can evoke the idea of continuity in time: the "ancient days" and the "years of old" are a model, a positive reference from the past (Malachi 3:4).
H6931H.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "before, in front," linked to the idea of what is ahead in time, thus what has preceded. Hebrew uses the same notion to evoke both the east (where the sun rises first) and the ancient (what has occurred first in time). This root also appears in other forms to express precedence and the past.
H6931H.emploi: The word appears four times in the Old Testament, in various contexts. It can qualify ancient wisdom or words (a proverb in 1 Samuel 24:14), a historical event or period that is past (Isaiah 43:18 and Malachi 3:4), or ancient prophetic words (Ezekiel 38:17). In each case, it marks a distance in time and invites the reader to consider what precedes the moment of speech. The meaning remains stable: what belongs to the past and has depth.
H6931H.portee: This word invites the believer to consider two attitudes toward the past. On one hand, the Bible recognizes the value of ancient things: the wisdom of the ancients, God's promises that date back far, the days of old when His grace was manifested. On the other hand, it calls not to remain imprisoned by the past: God offers something new, and the believer must sometimes let go of what is "ancient" to welcome what He prepares. It is a balance between respect for heritage and openness to divine novelty.

sens: City located east of the Jordan, in the territory of Reuben
Location assigned to the Levites of the family of Merari
H6932.detail: 1. Kedémoth is a city on the plateau east of the Jordan and the Dead Sea, in the territory of the tribe of Reuben. It is from a desert near this city that Moses sends messengers to King Sihon before the conquest (Deuteronomy 2:26). 2. The city is listed among the cities of the Reubenite territory (Joshua 13:18), and then it is given along with its surrounding lands to the Levites of the family of Merari, who serve in the tabernacle and the temple (Joshua 21:37 and 1 Chronicles 6:79).
H6932.origine: The name Kedémoth literally means "the ancient times" or "the east" in Hebrew, derived from the root "qedem" which denotes the east and also antiquity. This name reflects its geographical position to the east of the Jordan, in an ancient and well-established region.
H6932.emploi: Kedémoth appears four times in the Old Testament, always as a place name. It is first mentioned during the preparation for the conquest when Moses sends ambassadors to King Sihon (Deuteronomy 2:26). It is then included in the enumeration of the cities of Reuben (Joshua 13:18) and in the list of Levitical cities assigned to the family of Merari (Joshua 21:37 and 1 Chronicles 6:79, which repeats the same passage).

sens: Who comes first in order or succession
Who existed before, anciently or previously
H6933.detail:
1. Who comes first in order or succession: this is one who occupies the initial place or who occurs before others. In Daniel's vision, the first beast resembles a lion (Daniel 7:4); it is followed by other creatures, and when a new king arises, three of the first horns — the oldest or most powerful — are torn off (Daniel 7:8 and 7:24).
2. Who existed before, anciently or previously: the word describes what has occurred or what was established in an earlier time. The first kings of the kingdom are different from the one who comes after (Daniel 7:24): they belonged to a bygone era, while the new king who rises surpasses and replaces them.
H6933.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root קדם (qdm), which means "to go before" or "to precede." This root evokes the idea of what is ahead, what comes first, or what is ancient. The word is in adjective form and is used to qualify what occupies the first place chronologically or in the order of succession.
H6933.emploi: This word appears only three times in the Old Testament, all in the book of Daniel (7:4, 7:8, 7:24), in the context of the vision of the four symbolic beasts. Daniel describes a succession of kingdoms or kings: the first beast, then three of the first horns that are replaced. The word thus qualifies what comes first chronologically or hierarchically, before being surpassed or replaced by what follows. It is a vocabulary of prophetic vision that establishes a temporal and prophetic order.
H6933.portee: This word reminds the reader that the history of the world follows an order established by God, where powers and reigns succeed one another. Even the first things, which seem powerful and enduring, give way: what the prophetic vision reveals is that no human reign is definitive. For the believer, this invites one not to place trust in present powers, but to turn to the God who governs this succession and who remains beyond.

sens: Levite from the time of the return from exile after Babylon
Head of a family of Levites returned from captivity
Levite who oversaw the reconstruction of the temple
Levite who led the public confession of the people
H6934.detail:
1. Kadmiel is a Levite mentioned for the first time at the return from the Babylonian exile (Ezra 2:40), as the head of a family of seventy-four Levites, sons of Hodaviah, which shows his status as a family leader in the returning community.
2. He appears with Joshua and other Levites tasked with overseeing the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem (Ezra 3:9), showing that he was entrusted with important responsibilities in community endeavors.
3. Kadmiel is one of the figures who publicly leads the people to cry out to God and bless the Lord (Nehemiah 9:4-5), revealing his role as a spiritual leader and liturgist in the restored people.
4. His name means "God is the ancient one," which defines him in relation to the eternal divinity.
H6934.origine: The name Kadmiel is composed of two elements: "qadim" which means "ancient" or "of old," and "El" which means "God." It is a theological confession inscribed in a proper name: the one who bears this name affirms that God is eternal and unchanging. This type of theophoric name — containing the divine name — was common among the Hebrews to express their faith in God.
H6934.emploi: Kadmiel appears eight times in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, both narratives of the restoration after the Babylonian exile (586 B.C.). He is first listed among the heads of the Levitical families who accompanied the first return (Ezra 2:40 and Nehemiah 7:43 — the same list). He immediately stands out as responsible for the temple work with Joshua (Ezra 3:9). Later, Kadmiel is named among the Levites who publicly cry out the confession of the people (Nehemiah 9:4-5), and then who sign the covenant (Nehemiah 10:9). He is also found in the lists of Levitical singers of the temple (Nehemiah 12:8, 12:24). His constant presence in these spiritual and organizational roles shows that he was a stable and respected figure in the post-exilic restoration.
H6934.portee: Kadmiel embodies the role of the faithful Levite in the reconstruction of the community after the discipline of exile. His presence in every significant moment — the return, the reconstruction of the temple, the national confession — reminds us that God restores His people and once again places the spiritual heart of His community upon them, represented by the Levite. His name, "God is the ancient one," is a word of assurance for every believer in exile or trial: no matter how long the separation lasts, God remains eternal and faithful to bring back His people.

sens: Ancient people inhabiting Canaan
Descendants of Kadmon
The "Easterners" or peoples of the East
H6935.detail:
1. The Kadmonites are a people who occupied the land of Canaan before Abraham received it from God. They appear in the list of nations that God promises to drive out before Abraham's descendants (Genesis 15:19).
2. The name literally means "the ancients" or "those of the East," suggesting that this people was established in the eastern regions of Canaan or that they were an ancient population of the territory.
3. They symbolize the earthly and human obstacles that God's promise had to overcome: God promises Abraham not only a descendant but also the possession of the land, which implies the elimination of these established peoples.
H6935.origine: The name Kadmonite likely comes from a root meaning "ancient" or "eastern" (qedem in Hebrew = the east, antiquity). It is a people mentioned only once in the Bible, alongside other Canaanite peoples such as the Kenites and the Kenizzites. Unlike other Canaanite nations (the Amorites, the Hittites), the Kadmonites do not reappear anywhere else in the biblical narrative.
H6935.emploi: The Kadmonites are mentioned only once, in Genesis 15:19, in the context of God's covenant with Abram. This verse lists ten peoples (Kenites, Kenizzites, Kadmonites, Hittites, Perizzites, Rephaim, Amorites, Canaanites, Girgashites, and Jebusites) whose territory will be given to Abraham's descendants. This enumeration answers Abram's question: "How will I know that I will possess this land?" This single mention is enough to establish that the Kadmonites, although little known, are recognized by the Bible as a historical reality of ancient Canaan.
H6935.portee: For the Christian reader, the mention of the Kadmonites reminds us that the promise made to Abraham was not abstract: it concerned the concrete possession of a land occupied by real peoples. This illustrates how Abraham's faith was rooted in a specific and verifiable promise, even if these peoples seem obscure or forgotten by history. It is also a testimony to the reliability of God: He only promises what comes to pass.

sens: The highest part of the head
The hair of the skull
The highest point of the entire body
H6936.detail:
1. The word refers to the highest part of the human head, the highest point of the skull. It is the place where hair grows above the forehead. In Deuteronomy 28:35, we see that this top can be struck with sores, just as the soles of the feet are affected: it is the extreme point of the body, from top to bottom.
2. By extension, the word also evokes the hair itself, the crown of hair that covers the skull. In 2 Samuel 14:25, it is said that Absalom had no blemish "from the sole of his foot to the top of his head": this is a way of speaking about the entire body by emphasizing the two extremes, high and low.
3. The word also represents the peak, the summit, as in Genesis 49:26 where it is said that blessings rise "to the top of the eternal hills" and come "upon the top of the head of the prince of his brothers." It is the place where glory and blessing are concentrated.
H6936.origine: The Hebrew word קׇדְקֹד (qodqod) is a so-called "reduplicated" formation: a root is repeated to create a vivid image. This repetition suggests the idea of pointedness, crest, or crown. The same root appears in other Hebrew words related to what is high or pointed. This reduplicated process makes the image of the rounded and bulging top of the skull concrete and visible.
H6936.emploi: This word appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in narrative and poetic texts. It is often used in expressions that encompass the entire body, such as "from the sole of the foot to the top of the head" (Deuteronomy 28:35, 2 Samuel 14:25, Job 2:7), to show that a calamity or perfection extends from top to bottom without exception. It can also refer to the skull as the seat of the crown or blessing (Genesis 49:26, Deuteronomy 33:16). Less frequently, it represents the head as a target or distinguished part of the body (Isaiah 3:17, Jeremiah 2:16).
H6936.portee: This word reminds us that the entire body — from the highest to the lowest — can be affected by trials or divine blessing. It invites us to consider the body as an integrated whole. It also shows that the head is the seat of dignity and the crown: to bless someone on the head is to fill them with glory.

sens: To become dark, lose clarity (referring to the sky, light)
To take on a darkened, blackened hue (referring to a substance)
To be saddened, mourn (referring to a person or community)
To have the appearance of pain or sorrow
H6937.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: something bright becomes dark and obscure. In 1 Kings 18:45, the sky "darkens" with clouds during an approaching storm — it is the transition from light to darkness.
2. The word can refer to substances that take on a dark color. In Job 6:16, the "ice" or fragments of ice disturb the flow of a stream: the word here evokes their blackened or darkened appearance.
3. When referring to people, the word means to be weighed down by sadness or mourning. In Psalms 35:14, the psalmist says he drags himself with "sadness" as if mourning for a mother — his face and heart are darkened by grief.
4. The word also describes the external impression of misfortune and sorrow: Jeremiah 14:2 says that the cities of Judah are "sad" (or "darkened"), painting a picture where desolation has made the places gloomy and dark.
H6937.origine: The Hebrew root קדר (qadar) fundamentally evokes darkness and obscuring. It relates to the image of the transition from day to night, from light to dark. When it applies to humans or communities, it borrows this physical image of darkness to describe the emotional state: grief darkens the face and soul just as clouds darken the sky. The three verbal forms (Qal, Hiphil, Hithpael) allow for expressing both the action of becoming dark, causing to become dark, and allowing oneself to be darkened.
H6937.emploi: This verb appears 17 times in the Old Testament, primarily in poems (Psalms, Job) and the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Joel). It is first used for natural phenomena: the sky darkening in a storm (1 Kings 18:45, Joel 2:10), the stars darkened by divine anger (Ezekiel 32:7-8). Very often, it describes the state of mourning and misfortune: the people who are in sadness (Psalms 35:14, Jeremiah 14:2), the afflicted soul that bends down (Psalms 42:10). It is a word that physically associates darkness with moral or emotional darkness: where sorrow reigns, the world becomes dark.
H6937.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible uses images from the physical world to express the reality of emotions and spiritual states. Darkness is not just a matter of light: it is also mourning, oppression, judgment. For the reader, this shows how all of creation participates in the human drama — when the people suffer, even the heavens seem to darken. It is an invitation to see in the dark phenomena of spiritual life a reality that engages everything that exists.

sens: Son of Ishmael
Nomadic Arab people descended from Kedar
Region or territory inhabited by the Kedrites
H6938.detail:
1. Kedar is primarily the name of a son of Ishmael, listed among the twelve sons of the patriarch (Genesis 25:13 and 1 Chronicles 1:29).
2. The name then designates the nation or people of the Kedrites, descendants of this son, known as nomadic Arabs and shepherds living in the desert. Their name was associated with the characteristic black tents of the desert (Psalms 120:5; Song of Solomon 1:5).
3. Isaiah mentions the "valiant archers, sons of Kedar" (Isaiah 21:16-17), confirming that this people was renowned for their combat skills and nomadic life in arid regions.
H6938.origine: The name Kedar means "dark" or "black" in Hebrew, an image that evokes the black tents of the Bedouins of the desert. It is a patronymic that, as with Semitic nomads, became the name of the clan and the entire people formed by its descendants. The Kedrites inhabited the desert regions of western and northern Arabia, between Palestine and Mesopotamia.
H6938.emploi: Kedar appears about twelve times in the Hebrew Bible. Mentioned first in the genealogies of Ishmael (Genesis 25:13; 1 Chronicles 1:29), it quickly becomes a geographical and political term designating an established nomadic people. The psalms and prophets mention it to evoke desert life: the psalmist speaks with dismay of the "tents of Kedar" (Psalms 120:5), while in the Song of Solomon (1:5), these same tents symbolize dark beauty. Isaiah prophesies the ruin of the glory of Kedar (21:16-17), acknowledging their military and pastoral strength. Jeremiah and Ezekiel also mention them in oracles against the nations or in descriptions of trade.
H6938.portee: Kedar reminds the reader of the extent of Ishmael's descendants and the diversity of peoples in the ancient Near East. This nomadic people, by their constant presence at the borders of Israel, embodied a different world — that of the desert, nomadism, Arabia — and the prophets invoked them to express distant or inevitable realities. Understanding Kedar helps to geographically and culturally situate biblical episodes and prophetic visions.

sens: Stream that flows east of Jerusalem
Place of destruction of idols and objects of pagan worship
Symbol of separation and break from evil
H6939.detail:
1. The Kidron is a watercourse that runs through the valley east of Jerusalem, separating the city from the Mount of Olives. Its name means "dark" or "black," possibly evoking the murky waters of the stream or the darkness of the deep valley. It was by this stream that David fled during Absalom's rebellion, with all the people following him in tears (2 Samuel 15:23).
2. The Kidron is the place where the most pious kings of Judah destroyed the idols and worship utensils of false gods. Asa burned the idol of Ashtoreth made by his mother there (1 Kings 15:13), and King Josiah threw the ashes of the Baal idols and all the false worship objects there (2 Kings 23:4, 23:6, 23:12).
3. The Kidron stream thus becomes a symbol of definitive separation from idolatry: it is where one abandons, burns, and reduces to dust everything that diverts from God. Crossing or remaining on this side of the Kidron carries moral and spiritual significance in the history of Jerusalem.
H6939.origine: The Hebrew name קִדְרוֹן (qidron) literally means "dark" or "black," probably referring to the color of the waters of the stream or the austere appearance of the valley it traverses. It is a natural watercourse in the geography of Jerusalem, known since antiquity. The word is transliterated in Greek as Κέδρων (Kedron) in the Septuagint, and in Latin as Cedron in Latin versions.
H6939.emploi: The Kidron appears about ten times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the accounts of the kings of Judah. It is first mentioned as a stream to be crossed: David crosses it during his flight from Absalom, a moment of deep personal and national humiliation (2 Samuel 15:23). But it is especially memorable as a place of religious purification. The reforming kings — notably Asa, Hezekiah, and Josiah — threw and burned the objects of idolatrous worship there: idols of Ashtoreth, utensils dedicated to Baal, altars of false gods (1 Kings 15:13; 2 Kings 23:4, 23:6, 23:12; 2 Chronicles 29:16; 2 Chronicles 30:14). The Kidron thus became in the Old Testament the symbol of the irrevocable rejection of idolatry and the return to faithfulness to God.
H6939.portee: The Kidron reminds Christians that there are boundaries between what honors God and what dishonors Him. Just as the kings of Judah threw the idols into this stream to completely destroy them, believers are called to abandon without return everything that diverts them from God. It is a spiritual geography: remaining on this side of the Kidron or crossing it is to choose or deny one's belonging to God.

sens: Darkness, total or nearly total lack of light
Deep blackness of the sky or atmosphere
Figuratively: misfortune, mourning, sadness
H6940.detail:
1. Darkness refers to the absence of light, the state of complete darkness. In Isaiah 50:3, the Lord "clothes the heavens with darkness," speaking of how He can darken the sky as one would put on a garment of mourning.
2. It is also the visible blackness — the sky or atmosphere becoming dark and opaque, as if covered by a sack (cited verse). The image evokes not just a simple absence of sunlight, but a palpable covering of darkness.
3. In biblical language, darkness often symbolizes misfortune, sorrow, or mourning. Here, clothing the heavens with darkness and sack expresses mourning and divine judgment.
H6940.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be black, to become dark." It is related to other Hebrew words expressing blackness and darkness. The basic image is that of the color black and the absence of clarity.
H6940.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 50:3. It is found in a passage where the Lord asserts His power over creation: He can at will clothe the heavens with darkness and cover them as with a sack. The context is that of announcing the judgments or transformations that God performs, where the darkening of the sky symbolizes serious and solemn divine intervention.
H6940.portee: This word reminds us that darkness in Scripture is never a mere physical phenomenon: it speaks of misfortune, judgment, or the absence of divine clarity. Understanding that God controls the darkness and can use it for His purposes strengthens our trust in His sovereignty, even in the dark moments of our lives.

sens: State of dejection and sorrow
Affliction, mourning expressed by a somber attitude
Behavior of one who is burdened by the weight of their obligations
H6941.detail: 1. The word denotes a feeling of deep sadness and dejection, the state of a person who carries sorrow within. 2. It particularly evokes visible affliction, that which is expressed by a somber attitude, a bent posture — the demeanor of one who is crushed. 3. In its only biblical usage (Malachi 3:14), the word describes the Israelites who reproach God for having gained no profit from observing His precepts and walking "with sadness": it is the attitude of those who fulfill their religious duties not out of joy, but while dragging under the weight of obligation, without finding in this obedience any comfort or blessing.
H6941.origine: The word derives from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of bending, of being weighed down. The adjective expresses the state of one who is bent by grief, whose demeanor and heart bear the mark of sorrow. It is a rare word in the Old Testament, used to depict not only an inner feeling but also its bodily expression — visible sadness.
H6941.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Malachi 3:14. The Bible uses it to describe the spiritual posture of the Israelites during the time of the prophet Malachi, who accuse God of injustice. These men claim to have observed the Law and walked "with sadness" before God, that is, with rigorous devotion but without true heart, without joy. The sadness here is not that of authentic repentance, but that of burden — the bitterness of one who serves without love.
H6941.portee: This word reminds believers that serving God does not consist of fulfilling religious duties while dragging, with a heavy and bitter heart. True obedience must spring from a living relationship with God, a source of joy, not from a dreary and hopeless observance. It is an invitation to examine one's heart: do we serve God with eagerness and trust, or only out of obligation and resignation?

sens: set apart for God, reserved for His exclusive use
treat or regard as sacred, as belonging to God
separate from the profane, purify oneself
honor, revere someone as holy
observe a sacred limit, respect the forbidden
H6942G.detail:
1. To sanctify means primarily to reserve something or someone for God alone, setting it apart from the ordinary realm. This is what happens when the seventh day is sanctified (Genesis 2:3): this day becomes consecrated to God and separated from the others. Aaron and his sons are sanctified for the priesthood (Exodus 30:30), meaning they are set apart to serve God.
2. To sanctify also means to treat or regard something as sacred, as belonging to God and not to the profane. Thus, a priest is regarded as holy because he touches the food of God (Leviticus 21:8): he is treated with the respect due to one who is consecrated.
3. In certain contexts, to sanctify implies purifying oneself, separating from what defiles. Before approaching the Lord, the people must sanctify themselves (Exodus 19:10): they prepare by setting themselves apart from ordinary impurities.
4. The word can also mean to honor someone, to revere them as holy. When Moses did not sanctify God in the eyes of the people (Numbers 27:14), it means he did not honor Him, did not show His holiness.
5. Finally, to sanctify expresses the respect for a sacred limit or a prohibition, the observance of what is reserved for God. It is a protection of the sacred against the profane.
H6942G.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of separation, distinction. It is related to the adjective "qadosh" (holy), which designates what is separated, set apart, and fundamentally what is sacred because distinct from the ordinary world. The root expresses a cut, a limit between two realms: the sacred and the profane. The central idea is that of separation and setting apart for divine use.
H6942G.emploi: This verb is one of the most important in the ritual vocabulary of the Old Testament: it appears 113 times, notably in Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers. It primarily describes God's actions: God sanctifies the Sabbath day (Genesis 2:3), He sanctifies His temple (2 Chronicles 7:16). It also describes the actions of people towards God: we sanctify the Lord by respecting Him, treating Him as sacred (Leviticus 22:32). The word applies to objects (the altar must be sanctified, Exodus 29:37), to people (the priests, Exodus 28:41), to days (the Sabbath, Deuteronomy 5:12), and to the entire people called to sanctify themselves (Leviticus 20:7). Depending on the contexts, to sanctify can be an act of ritual consecration or an act of reverence and honor.
H6942G.portee: This word teaches us a decisive truth: holiness does not primarily mean moral perfection, but being set apart for God, separation from the profane. When the Bible calls me to sanctify myself, it invites me to set myself apart for God, to cease being "ordinary" in His hands, to recognize that I am reserved for His use. What is sanctified belongs to God and must be treated with a respect that reflects this special status. It is a call to honor the Lord as God, and to live in awareness of this separation.

sens: Set apart something or someone for God's use, removing it from ordinary use
Declare or treat something as holy, sacred, reserved for God
Solemnly dedicate a possession, a property, a child to the Lord
Stand oneself apart, sanctify oneself, speaking of a person who dedicates themselves to God
H6942H.detail:
1. To consecrate means to remove something from its ordinary use to reserve it for God alone. In Leviticus 27:14, a house that is "sanctified" becomes God's property and can no longer serve ordinary needs. The act of consecration marks a separation: what was profane becomes sacred.

2. To treat something as holy means to respect it as belonging to God and to honor it. In Exodus 13:2, God requires that every firstborn be consecrated, meaning treated with reverence as His personal property.

3. Dedicating a possession to God means solemnly giving it as a gift. In 1 Chronicles 18:11, David "consecrates" the gold and silver taken from the enemies: he transfers ownership to the house of the Lord, where this money will serve for worship.

4. For a person, to consecrate oneself or to be consecrated to God means to devote oneself to His service, to live being set apart for Him. This is the case for one who makes a Nazarite vow or for a priest destined for temple ministry.
H6942H.origine: The Hebrew word qdsh (קדש) comes from a root that means "to separate," "to withdraw." The central idea is that of separation from the profane: what is qodash (holy, consecrated) is separated, set apart, distinct. The noun qodesh (holiness, sanctuary) and the adjective qadosh (holy, sacred) come from the same root. The Greek hagiazo (ἁγιάζω) regularly translates this word in the Septuagint, retaining the idea of sacred separation.
H6942H.emploi: This verb appears 22 times in biblical Hebrew, especially in the Law (Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy) and in the accounts of the kings of Judah. It expresses the action of reserving for God: a house, a field, war booty, an animal, or a person. Sometimes the king or the people consecrate a possession (2 Samuel 8:11, 1 Chronicles 26:27), sometimes the Lord Himself consecrates, that is, manifests Himself as holy (Ezekiel 36:23, implicitly in the uses of the Hithpael). The verb also designates the action of being consecrated, becoming sacred: which can be a passive transformation (being set apart) or the action of a person who separates themselves for God. The context always shows that it is a solemn, definitive action that engages both God and man.
H6942H.portee: For today's believer, to consecrate is not limited to the rituals of the Temple: it is to recognize that everything comes from God and to place one's possessions, time, and life in His hands. Jeremiah 1:5, where God says to Jeremiah, "I have consecrated you," shows that consecration is also a calling: God chooses us and sets us apart for a mission. To consecrate reminds us that separation from sin and obedience to God are not constraints, but the honor of becoming His instruments.

sens: To lose or be unable to use a good or its fruit
To be deprived of the use or benefit of something
H6942I.detail:
1. In Deuteronomy 22:9, "enjoy" means to benefit from or enjoy the produce: the text forbids sowing mixed seeds in a vineyard; otherwise, one will not enjoy either the produce of the seeds or the produce of the vineyard. The word evokes the idea of losing or being deprived of the fruit of one's labor as a consequence of violating the law.
2. More broadly, the Hebrew verb קָדַשׁ (qadash) expresses separation or consecration: what is consecrated to God is set apart, separated from ordinary use. Here, in this legal context, the idea is that if one mixes two holy things (the seed and the vineyard), one becomes unable to enjoy (to use or benefit from) either one.
H6942I.origine: The verb קָדַשׁ (qadash) comes from a root that fundamentally means "to separate," "to set apart." Throughout the Pentateuch and the books of the Old Testament, this verb primarily denotes the action of consecrating an object, a person, or a time to God, that is, isolating them from the profane and reserving them for the sacred. The root conveys the image of a boundary or separation: what is qadosh (holy) is distinct from the ordinary world. The derived noun קֹדֶשׁ (qodesh) means "holiness" or "sanctuary."
H6942I.emploi: The verb קָדַשׁ appears only once in the Segond with the translation "enjoy" in Deuteronomy 22:9. Elsewhere in the Old Testament, this verb is rendered as "consecrate," "sanctify," "hallow," or "dedicate" depending on the contexts. The translation "enjoy" is rare and specific: it reflects here the meaning of "benefit," that is, the opposite consequence of sanctification. When something is consecrated or set apart in a forbidden manner (like the mixing of seeds), one is deprived (one does not "enjoy") of its use or fruit. It is a legal consequence of failing to respect the separation that God requires.
H6942I.portee: This passage teaches that God desires order and purity even in the ordinary details of life (the cultivation of the vineyard). The prohibition against mixing seeds is not arbitrary: it reminds us that God separates the holy from the profane, and that this separation applies everywhere. The Christian will find an invitation to holiness and faithfulness to God, even in small things, knowing that disrespecting divine order has concrete consequences: one loses the blessing and the fruit of one's labor.

sens: To set apart for God, to make holy and separate from the profane
To prepare, organize for an action
To publish, announce openly
To treat with respect and reverence
H6942J.detail:
1. To set apart for God, to make holy and separate from the profane: this means reserving something or someone exclusively for divine service, removing it from ordinary use. In Joshua 20:7, the cities of refuge are "consecrated" as holy places where the involuntary murderer can find protection — they become separated spaces, marked by God's will.
2. To prepare, organize for an action: the word also means to gather forces or means to accomplish something decisive. In Jeremiah 22:7, God "prepares" destroyers against Jerusalem, meaning He organizes them, positions them for battle. The same meaning is found in Jeremiah 51:27-28: "Prepare the nations," meaning assemble them, put them in position.
3. To publish, announce openly: in Micah 3:5, the false prophets "publish war" when they are paid — they announce publicly, making it known to all.
4. To treat with respect and reverence: to honor, to recognize as sacred. This is the inner attitude that often accompanies consecration.
H6942J.origine: The Hebrew verb קָדַשׁ (qadash) comes from a root that fundamentally means "to be separated, set apart." It is related to the word קדֹשׁ (qadosh, "holy"), which designates what is separated from the profane and belongs to God. The starting image is therefore one of separation, of setting aside. The entire family of this word revolves around the idea of holiness and cultic separation: what is consecrated is what is removed from ordinary circulation to belong to God.
H6942J.emploi: The verb appears seven times in the provided usages, mostly in Jeremiah. In three cases (Jeremiah 6:4, 51:27, 51:28), it means "to prepare" an army or a siege: to gather, to organize military forces. In Joshua 20:7, it concerns consecrating the cities of refuge, officially establishing them as holy places. In Jeremiah 12:3 and 22:7, "to prepare" means to destine for destruction: it is to prepare for judgment. In Micah 3:5, "to publish" war means to announce it, to proclaim it. The word thus always retains the idea of separating, establishing, organizing for a purpose — whether it be holy or warrior-like.
H6942J.portee: This word reminds us that biblical consecration is never purely personal: it signifies a public setting apart, an orientation of one's life towards the service of God. For the believer, to be consecrated is to be prepared by God for His purposes, just as the cities of refuge were for the protection of the innocent. It is also an invitation not to keep for oneself what has been entrusted: to announce, publish, and implement what God has established.

sens: To set apart, consecrate something or someone for God
To be holy, separated from evil and sin
To treat or recognize as sacred, worthy of respect
To show oneself holy and powerful through one's acts
To keep, observe something as sacred
H6942K.detail:
1. To sanctify means to set apart for God, to reserve for His service. This can concern an object, a time, or a person: one separates it from the profane, from the common, to dedicate it to God. Example: the people of Israel that God will gather and consecrate for His name (Ezekiel 28:25).
2. It also means to be holy, that is, pure and separated from evil, without compromise with sin. When it is said that God is sanctified, it is affirmed that He is absolutely holy, that no one can compare to Him.
3. To sanctify means to recognize as sacred, to treat with respect and reverence what belongs to God. The nations must learn to treat God Himself as holy, to truly respect Him.
4. God also sanctifies Himself by manifesting His holiness through His powerful judgments: when He acts to punish evil and bring justice, He shows that He is holy and does not tolerate sin. In Ezekiel 28:22, God says, "I will manifest My holiness in her" through His judgments against Sidon.
5. To observe something as sacred means to keep it separate, to protect it from any defilement. It is to maintain the distinction between what is holy and what is profane.
H6942K.origine: The Hebrew root qdsh expresses the fundamental idea of separation, of setting apart. The word belongs to a family that also produces "qodesh" (holiness, holy place) and "qadosh" (holy). In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), this Hebrew verb is almost always translated by the Greek verb "hagiazô," from the same family as "hagios" (holy). The starting image is that of a limit or boundary: what is holy is separated from the rest, marked as belonging exclusively to God.
H6942K.emploi: This verb appears 9 times in the Segond, always in the book of Ezekiel, in the promises and acts of God regarding Israel and the nations. God declares that He will "sanctify" His great name that has been profaned (Ezekiel 36:23), meaning He will restore the respect that the nations owe to His name through His powerful acts. He also promises to manifest His holiness through the fulfillment of His plans: when He gathers Israel and judges its enemies, the nations will know that He is the Lord (Ezekiel 28:22-25; 38:16,23). The word expresses both God's act (setting apart Israel for His service) and the revelation of His holy nature through His judgments. Ezekiel 44:19 mentions the obligation not to sanctify (profaning by making them holy) the garments in contact with the people — a specific usage related to temple service.
H6942K.portee: This word calls the reader to understand that God's holiness is not a distant abstraction: it is manifested through His acts and concrete judgments towards His people and His enemies. To sanctify His name is to treat it as the unique and all-powerful God that He is, and to recognize that what happens in history — the salvation of the people, the judgment of evil — reveals His holiness. It also invites the Christian to allow themselves to be sanctified, to be set apart for God and consecrated to His service.

sens: Fortified city in Galilee
City of refuge for murderers
Military gathering place in Israel
H6943G.detail:
1. Kedesh is a fortified city located in Galilee, in the mountainous region of Naphtali (Joshua 20:7). Its name means "holy place" or "sanctuary," evoking a location dedicated to God. It is among the Canaanite cities conquered by Israel and listed in the accounts of Joshua (Joshua 12:22).

2. After the conquest, Kedesh was designated as a city of refuge for unintentional murderers (Joshua 21:32). These cities provided legal protection for those who had accidentally killed someone, allowing them to escape family vengeance until a fair judgment could be made.

3. Kedesh also served as a military rallying point: the prophetess Deborah and the leader Barak gathered ten thousand warriors there before fighting Sisera and his chariots (Judges 4:9-10). Thus, it embodied a strategic and religious center of life in Israel.
H6943G.origine: The name qedesh comes from a Hebrew root meaning "holiness" or "consecration." This root appears throughout the Bible to designate anything that is separated, reserved for God, or different from the profane. Therefore, Kedesh carries a theological name: it is a "holy place," likely an ancient Canaanite sanctuary taken over by Israel and integrated into its religious and political system.
H6943G.emploi: Kedesh appears nine times in the Hebrew Bible, always as a proper name designating a specific city. It first appears in the conquest lists (Joshua 12:22), then in the division of territories (Joshua 19:37) and the allocation of Levitical cities (Joshua 21:32). It gains historical significance in the account of Deborah and Barak (Judges 4:9-10), where it becomes the site of the decisive gathering against Sisera. It is also mentioned in later royal annals (2 Kings 15:29, 1 Chronicles 6:76), confirming its constant role in the political and religious life of northern Israel.
H6943G.portee: Kedesh illustrates how God established structures of justice and refuge at the heart of Israel's life. The designation of a city of refuge shows that divine law protected the innocent and tempered human vengeance. Kedesh's role in Deborah's campaign also reminds us that it was by gathering in places of worship and under the guidance of prophets that the people found the strength to overcome their enemies.

sens: City in the southern part of Judah
H6943H.detail: Kedesh is a city located in the extreme south of the territory of Judah, listed among the cities that this people was to occupy after the conquest (Joshua 15:23). Its name means "holy place" in Hebrew, but here it simply designates a geographical locality.
H6943H.origine: The Hebrew name קֶדֶשׁ (qedesh) comes from the root קדש (qdsh) which means "to be holy" or "to be consecrated." This same word elsewhere designates a "holy place" or a sanctuary. Here it carries a name that likely recalls its sacred character or a sanctuary that was established there.
H6943H.emploi: Kedesh appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:23, where it is listed among the cities of the Negev (the desert region in the south) that Judah was to conquer and inhabit. This enumeration shows how the promised territory to the tribe of Judah was divided into urban domains after entering the Promised Land.

sens: City of refuge in northern Galilee, in the territory of Naphtali
H6943I.detail: Kedesh is one of the six cities of refuge that God established in Israel to protect someone who accidentally killed another person (Numbers 35). Its name means "holy place" in Hebrew, and it was located in the northern part of the country, in the region of Galilee. It served as a refuge for those who had committed unintentional homicide and needed to flee from the avenger of blood. In 1 Chronicles 6:72, it is mentioned among the cities assigned to the Levites: "from the tribe of Issachar, Kedesh and its pasturelands, Dobrath and its pasturelands." It is another name for Kishion, the original city of this region.
H6943I.origine: The name Kedesh comes from the Hebrew root qadash (קדש), which means "to be holy, to be consecrated." It was a name carrying religious significance: by establishing a city of refuge called "holy place," God indicated that this refuge was a sacred space, placed under His divine protection, where the unintentional murderer could find safety.
H6943I.emploi: Kedesh is mentioned only once in the Bible (1 Chronicles 6:72) as a city assigned to the Levites, from the tribe of Issachar. It is one of the cities of refuge established by God to offer asylum to unintentional murderers, who remained there until judgment or the death of the high priest. Its status as a holy place reminded that even divine justice was merciful toward one who did not intend to kill.
H6943I.portee: Kedesh symbolizes God's mercy toward unintentional sinners: God does not condemn one who has committed a fault without malicious intent, but offers them refuge and protection. It is a biblical image of grace toward one who does not deserve punishment.

sens: Fortified city in Canaan allotted to the tribe of Naphtali
H6943J.detail: 1. Kedesh-Naphtali is a fortified city located in Canaan, in the territory assigned to the tribe of Naphtali. Its name means "holy place" in Hebrew, revealing its religious or symbolic importance for Israel. It is from this city that the prophetess Deborah calls Barak to rise up against the army of Sisera (Judges 4:6).
H6943J.origine: The name Kedesh comes from the Hebrew root *qadosh*, which means "holy" or "consecrated." It is a place where divine holiness is expressed. Several cities bore this name in Israel — there was also a Kedesh in the Negev and another in Galilee — but this one, Kedesh-Naphtali, is specifically the one in the north, in the territory of Naphtali.
H6943J.emploi: Kedesh-Naphtali appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 4:6, at a key moment in Israel's history. It is the starting point of a major liberation: the prophetess Deborah sends for Barak to rise up against Sisera and his army. This city served as a strategic and religious base for the Israelite leaders of the north. Its name, "holy place," emphasizes that even in military struggles for independence, God sanctifies His actions and His places.
H6943J.portee: Kedesh-Naphtali reminds us that God used concrete places and people to accomplish His deliverance. It is from a small fortified city that the call to victory over a powerful enemy emerged. For the reader, this name speaks of God's closeness in daily struggles: the Lord does not only reign in heaven, but acts through cities, judges, and warriors to save His people.

sens: Separated, set apart in a special way for God
Pure, free from defilement
Belonging to God or intended for His worship
To be treated with respect and reverence
The entirety of places and objects consecrated for worship (the sanctuary)
H6944G.detail:
1. The word "holy" primarily refers to something or someone that is separated, set aside for a special use: God tells Moses, "the place on which you stand is holy ground" (Exodus 3:5), meaning that this place is reserved for His presence and must be approached with fear.
2. An object or person is "holy" when it is pure and free from ritual contamination: an offering that remains from burnt sacrifices is "most holy" and may only be eaten under prescribed conditions (Leviticus 10:12).
3. The word qualifies what is God's property or dedicated to His service: the utensils of the sanctuary, the garments of the priests, the anointing oil—all of these are "holy" because they are intended for the worship of the Lord (Exodus 28:2, Exodus 30:25).
4. "Holy" also expresses the attitude one must have towards consecrated things: they must be treated with deference, not touched lightly, and the prohibitions concerning them must be respected.
5. The "sanctuary" itself is the holy place par excellence, the space reserved for God in the tabernacle, where His presence resides (Numbers 4:12).
H6944G.origine: The Hebrew word קֹדֶשׁ comes from a root that originally means "to cut, to separate": to be holy is to be separated, set apart. This idea of separation is fundamental: holiness is not primarily a morality, but a ritual condition of separation from the profane. The same root has given rise to "sanctuary," and the verbs "to consecrate" or "to dedicate" which express the action of making something holy. In Israel, holiness characterizes God Himself, who is separated from all creation, and then radiates onto the places, objects, and people that are consecrated to Him.
H6944G.emploi: This word is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible: 346 occurrences. It appears mainly in Exodus and Leviticus, where it qualifies the sanctuary, its garments, its utensils, and the offerings (Exodus 28, Exodus 30, Leviticus 2 to 7, Leviticus 16). In the Psalms and the prophets, it describes God's mountain, the feasts (Exodus 12:16), and the call of the people to holiness (Exodus 15:11: "Who is like you among the gods, O Lord? Who is like you, majestic in holiness?"). The word also applies to what one voluntarily dedicates to God (Ezekiel 20:40: "all that you dedicate to me"). The priests and the people of Israel are called to be holy, that is, separated and available for God.
H6944G.portee: The holiness of God reveals that we cannot approach Him casually, that His presence demands respect, purity, and reverence. For the believer, this word teaches that everything dedicated to God—our bodies, our possessions, our time—must be treated as sacred and separated from evil. It also tells us that we are called to share in this holiness: to be holy is to be set apart for God, living differently from the world that ignores Him.

sens: Sacred space, reserved for God, separated from the rest of ordinary life
Inner chamber of the temple, the most holy, where the ark of the covenant rested
Quality of what is pure, holy, set apart for God
H6944H.detail:
1. The word "sanctuary" first evokes a separation: what is sacred is set apart, isolated from what is profane. This is the fundamental meaning of the Hebrew word, which speaks of something apart, "set aside" for God alone. In 1 Chronicles 6:49, Aaron and his sons perform their duties "in the most holy place": it is a reserved space, forbidden to others, entirely devoted to divine service.
2. In the temple of Jerusalem, the sanctuary specifically refers to the innermost room, the "Holy of Holies," where the ark of the covenant was located. In 1 Kings 8:6, "the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the Lord to its place, in the sanctuary of the house, in the Holy of Holies, under the wings of the cherubim." This chamber was so sacred that only the high priest could enter it once a year.
3. The word can also more broadly designate the quality of holiness, what makes something sacred and worthy of respect. It is the state of being set apart for God, being pure and consecrated.
H6944H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to be apart, to be separated." The central idea is the separation from the profane: what is sacred is removed from ordinary use. This root also produces the words "holy" and "holiness." In Greek, the New Testament often renders this concept with the word ἅγιον (hagion, "the most holy"), which carries the same idea of sacred separation.
H6944H.emploi: The word appears about ten times in the Bible, almost exclusively in accounts of the construction and use of the temple (1 and 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles) and in prophetic descriptions of the future temple (Ezekiel). It constantly designates the innermost chamber of the temple of Jerusalem, the most holy, where the ark of the covenant containing the tablets of the Law rested. In 1 Kings 6:16, it is stated, "this space is reserved to make the sanctuary, the most holy place." In 2 Chronicles 3:8-10, the two sculpted cherubim are added there. The word always emphasizes the idea of absolute separation and maximum sacredness.
H6944H.portee: For the believer, the sanctuary reminds us that God is infinitely holy and that communion with Him requires purity. The heavenly temple revealed in Revelation maintains the same sacred structure. For Christians, the body itself becomes a "temple of the Holy Spirit," a living sanctuary: we are called to live in a state of separation from sin, consecrated to God.

sens: Separated, set apart for God
Consecrated, reserved for sacred use
Pure, without defilement
Worthy of respect and reverence for God
H6944I.detail:
1. The word first expresses the idea of separation: something that is set apart, removed from common use to belong to God alone. The "holy" way of Isaiah 35:8 is reserved for the redeemed; it is separated from the ordinary path of the unclean.

2. It also means being consecrated, dedicated to God with a solemn intention. Holiness is not merely a moral quality, but a status: what is holy has been set apart for God and cannot be used for other purposes.

3. To be holy is also to be pure, without contamination or defilement. On the holy way of Isaiah, only those who are purified may pass; the unclean are excluded by nature.

4. Finally, holiness inspires reverence, respectful fear: what is holy demands respect and calls for an attitude of worship. The holy way is not a mere road, but a path that inspires admiration and submission.
H6944I.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to cut, to separate." The basic image is that of separation: what is holy is cut off, isolated, removed from the realm of the profane to be reserved for God. This root is used in various contexts: for holy places (the temple, the sanctuary), sacred objects (the altar, the ark), and consecrated persons (priests, prophets). The word also has a moral sense: the holiness of God expresses His absolutely pure character, separated from evil.
H6944I.emploi: This word appears very frequently in the Old Testament to designate everything that belongs to God and is reserved for Him: holy places, objects of worship, sacred days, and the people of Israel themselves, called to be a holy nation. In the passage of Isaiah 35:8, it qualifies the way of the return of the redeemed: this road is not ordinary; it is holy because it is intended for God's elect, purified and separated from all that is impure. The context shows that holiness is both a reality that separates the unclean and a promise: those who follow this way will not go astray.
H6944I.portee: Understanding holiness as separation for God changes the believer's perspective. It is not primarily a moral perfection that we must achieve, but a call to be set apart, consecrated to God. The holy way promised in Isaiah speaks of the security and direction that God gives to His people. For the Christian, this means that holiness is a vocation: to be holy is to be separated from the world and devoted to God, a reality that inspires both trust and respectful obedience.

sens: Space dedicated to God in the temple or the tent of meeting
Part of the sanctuary reserved for the priests
What is separated, set apart for sacred use
Character of what is holy, separated from the profane
H6944J.detail:
1. The sanctuary is primarily the building or tent itself where God dwells and where one meets Him. It is a place set apart, reserved solely for Him: "You shall put the veil under the clasps, and the ark of the testimony shall be brought in there, behind the veil; the veil shall serve as a separation between the holy place and the most holy place" (Exodus 26:33). 
2. The word also designates, more specifically, the front part of the sanctuary, where the priests enter to serve (distinct from the "most holy place" or holy of holies): "They shall be carried by the one of his sons who succeeds him in the priesthood for seven days, and he shall enter the tent of meeting to minister in the sanctuary" (Exodus 29:30).
3. The sanctuary is a space of absolute holiness, where strict rules prevail: no one may enter in any manner or dressed in any way. The garments themselves are called "sacred" because they are intended for service in this place (Exodus 39:41).
4. The word evokes the idea of separation: it is a place set apart, removed from the ordinary world, where the profane has no access. This separation creates a respectful distance between God and humanity, reminding us that God is totally different, completely other.
H6944J.origine: The Hebrew word קֹ֫דֶשׁ (qodesh) comes from a root that means "to cut," "to separate." The central idea is that of separation, of being set apart. Something holy is something that has been separated from the profane, reserved for God alone. Words from the same family designate holiness, the sacred character, or consecrated persons. In Greek, this word is often translated as ἅγιον (hagion), "holy place," which carries the same idea of separation and consecration.
H6944J.emploi: This word appears 26 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books of the Law (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers) and in the accounts of the kings and Chronicles. It primarily designates the tent of meeting (or tabernacle) and later the temple of Jerusalem. Its various uses show how the sanctuary is the center of Israel's religious life: sacrifices are offered there, the ark of the covenant is kept there, and only the priests can access it under certain conditions. In the passages from Kings and Chronicles, the sanctuary appears as the heart of the worship of the true God, and neglecting the sanctuary is turning away from God Himself (2 Chronicles 29:7).
H6944J.portee: For the Christian, the sanctuary reminds us that God demands a separation between the sacred and the profane, and that one does not approach God in just any manner. The New Testament teaches that Jesus Christ is the true living sanctuary, and that believers together form a spiritual temple of God. Meditating on the holiness of the sanctuary awakens respect for God and the importance of personal consecration.

sens: Man engaged in prostitution in a religious or idolatrous worship context
Person of dissolute or depraved morals
H6945.detail:
1. The word designates a man who engages in prostitution, generally within the framework of an idolatrous worship or pagan religious practices. In 1 Kings 14:24, we see that such "prostitutes" existed in Israel, imitating the abominations of neighboring nations; they were part of the corrupt religious system worshipped by idolaters. King Asa and his successors pursued the elimination of these practices (1 Kings 15:12; 1 Kings 22:47), and King Josiah destroyed even the buildings where they operated, notably next to the temple of the Lord (2 Kings 23:7).
2. In a broader sense, the word can simply mean a debauched person, someone whose life is marked by vice and immorality. In Job 36:14, the "debauched" are those who waste their lives in youth because of their dissolute morals, without a specific cultic context mentioned.
H6945.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that primarily evokes separation or consecration (hence positive derivatives like "holy" or "sanctuary"). But here, the word designates someone who has "separated" or set apart for religious prostitution — a radical profanation of sacred meaning. The Segond translation reflects this contrast by using the term "prostitute" for clearly ritual passages and "debauched" for the general moral image.
H6945.emploi: The word appears 6 times, mainly in the historical books (1 Kings and 2 Kings) and once in Job. It designates a practice that is both religious and moral, characteristic of the worship of the nations that the Lord drove out of Israel. The Law explicitly forbids this practice in Israel (Deuteronomy 23:17). The pious kings fought against it: Asa removed it from the land, and Josiah demolished the buildings where it was practiced near the temple. The word thus carries a dimension of ritual abomination and unfaithfulness to the Lord.
H6945.portee: This word reminds the reader that sexual sin is never private or personal: it often roots itself in idolatry and corrupts the worship rendered to the Lord. It also shows that God demands a moral purity from His people that is radically different from the practices of neighboring nations. The tenacity of the righteous kings to eradicate this practice underscores the importance that the Law attaches to the holiness of the body and fidelity in worship.

sens: Oasis in the Sinai desert, in the far south of the territory of Israel
Major stopping place during the forty years of wandering of the people after the exodus from Egypt
H6946G.detail:
1. Kadesh is an oasis located in the desert of Zin, at the southernmost tip of the territory that God destined for Israel. It is a strategic water point: Abraham passed through there (Genesis 20:1), and it marked the borders of the promised land (Numbers 20:16).
2. Kadesh becomes the heart of the people's experience in the desert: the Israelites camp there for a long time after leaving Egypt, and it is there that decisive events occur — the death of Miriam (Numbers 20:1), the rebellion against God's command during the "contention over the waters" (Numbers 27:14) — which delay entry into the Promised Land by forty years.
H6946G.origine: The name "Kadesh" means "holiness" or "sacred" in Hebrew, from the root qdsh. It is a name that underscores the religious significance of the place: it is where God powerfully intervenes in the life of Israel, where He manifests His holiness through signs and judgments.
H6946G.emploi: Kadesh is mentioned 15 times in the Bible, mainly in the books of Numbers and Deuteronomy that recount the exodus and the wandering in the desert. It also appears in Genesis as a stop for Abraham, and in Judges during border conflicts. It is primarily a refuge (Genesis 20:1, Genesis 14:7), then the site of the people's spiritual crises: rebellion, lack of faith, and divine judgment that prolongs the exodus by forty years. Kadesh embodies the place where Israel learns obedience to God through trials.
H6946G.portee: Kadesh reminds the Christian that God tests His people to strengthen their faith. It is a place where obedience or rebellion has lasting consequences: murmuring against God costs forty years in the desert. For the believer, Kadesh symbolizes the difficult passages of spiritual life, where God confronts us with our lack of trust and calls us to grow in faith.

sens: Oasis in the desert of Sinai, in the southern part of the Promised Land
Place where Israel stayed for a long time during the Exodus
Southern boundary of the territory of Israel
H6946H.detail:
1. Kadesh is an oasis located in the desert of Sinai, in the extreme southern part of the region where Israel was to enter. The name means "holy" and designates this place considered sacred. It is an important water source in an arid desert.

2. During the Exodus, the people of Israel stayed a long time at Kadesh, where several major events took place: Moses struck the rock to bring forth water (the waters of Meribah, meaning "strife"), and it was here that God rebuked Moses and Aaron for not having sanctified Him before the people (Deuteronomy 32:51).

3. In the geography of the future territory of Israel, Kadesh marks the southern limit: it is the starting point of the territory defining the southern boundaries of the Promised Land, as indicated by the descriptions in Ezekiel (47:19 and 48:28).
H6946H.origine: The name קָדֵשׁ (Kadesh) literally means "holy" or "sanctified" in Hebrew, derived from the root קדש (qdsh) which evokes separation and consecration. This place bears this name because it was considered a consecrated site. The same location is also referred to as Kadesh-Barnea or Kédesh in other biblical texts.
H6946H.emploi: Kadesh appears three times in the translations of the Segond, always in relation to "Meribah" ("Meribah" in English), hence the full name "Kadesh-Meribah." In Deuteronomy 32:51, Moses reminds the people that it was there that the Israelites sinned and that God was not sanctified among them. The two passages in Ezekiel (47:19 and 48:28) describe Kadesh as a landmark of the southern boundary of the territory of Israel, marking the limit between the Promised Land and the desert. Kadesh is thus both a historical site of the Exodus desert and a constant geographical reference for delineating the territory of Israel.
H6946H.portee: Kadesh reminds the Christian reader of both the weakness of Israel and the patience of God during the Exodus: it is a place where the people murmured and sinned, but also where God provided for their needs for water. The name "holy" of this place evokes that even in the heart of the desert and trial, God marks His people with the seal of consecration and maintains their boundaries. It is a reminder that all limits and territory belong to God alone.

sens: Oasis and city in the southern desert of Sinai
Base of operations for the Israelites during their desert crossing
H6947.detail:
1. Kadesh-Barnea is an oasis located in the southern Sinai, at the borders of the territory of Judah. It is a water source in the desert, strategically important for travelers and armies crossing these arid regions (Numbers 34:4; Joshua 15:3).
2. It is primarily the starting point from which Moses sent the twelve spies to explore the land of Canaan, and the place where the Israelites received the discouraging report that led to their rebellion against God. Because of this unbelief, they had to wander for forty years in the desert instead of entering Canaan immediately (Numbers 32:8; Deuteronomy 9:23).
H6947.origine: The name Kadesh-Barnea means "Kadesh the holy," from the Hebrew word *qadesh* ("sanctuary" or "consecrated place"), combined with *Barnea*, a term possibly designating a spring or region. Kadesh often appears in the Bible for consecrated places, notably the oasis in the desert of Sinai.
H6947.emploi: Kadesh-Barnea appears about ten times in the Pentateuch and the beginning of the Deuteronomistic history. It is mentioned as a geographical reference point (Deuteronomy 1:2 — eleven days from Horeb), as a place of prolonged encampment for the Israelites (Deuteronomy 2:14 — thirty-eight years between Kadesh-Barnea and the Zered), and especially as the theater of the refusal to go and conquer Canaan. This event is recalled several times to show how the desert generation lacked faith (Joshua 14:6-7 — Caleb testifies to what he saw and believed at Kadesh-Barnea).
H6947.portee: Kadesh-Barnea symbolizes in the Bible the decisive moment when faith confronts fear. It is here that the Israelites, despite God's promises and evidence of His power, succumbed to doubt by believing the bad news rather than the divine word. This account challenges the believer on the importance of trusting God in the face of difficulties, and on the consequences of unbelief: an entire generation missed the fulfillment of God's promises.

sens: Woman who engages in prostitution, particularly in the context of idolatrous worship or moral disorder
Adulterous or debauched woman associated with pagan religious practices
H6948.detail: 1. The term designates a woman who prostitutes herself, often in connection with false religious rituals or idolatrous cults. In Genesis 38:21-22, Judah seeks "this prostitute" who had been standing by the roadside — it refers to Tamar in disguise, and the term underscores the apparent dishonor of the situation. 2. The Law of Israel categorically prohibits this practice: "There shall be no prostitute among the daughters of Israel" (Deuteronomy 23:17). God's people must avoid it, as it is incompatible with the covenant with the Lord. 3. In Hosea 4:14, the prophet denounces those "who go aside with prostitutes and sacrifice with debauched women": he shows how sexual immorality and idolatry are closely linked. The term reveals that these women are not merely ordinary prostitutes, but actors in false worship that corrupts Israel.
H6948.origine: The word comes from the root qadash, which primarily means "to be consecrated" or "to be set apart for worship." But applied to a woman, it has an inverted and ironic meaning: instead of being consecrated to the true God, she is "consecrated" (in appearance) to false worship, that is, she prostitutes herself. It is a distortion of religious language to describe the worst moral disorder.
H6948.emploi: The term appears 4 times in the Hebrew Bible, only in the Law and the Prophets. Twice in Genesis 38, in the story of Judah and Tamar, where the term serves to describe the supposed condition of the one who stood by the way. Once in Deuteronomy 23:17, where the Law formally prohibits this practice among the Israelites. Once in Hosea 4:14, where the prophet denounces the men of Israel who go to these women and commit idolatry. In each usage, the term underscores not only sexual immorality but also religious corruption and the refusal of the covenant with God.
H6948.portee: This term reminds the believer that sexuality is a gift from God, inseparable from His covenant and holiness. It also shows how idolatry and sexual immorality walk together: to divert love and the body from God's plan is to fall into idolatry. It is a warning against false worship that promises freedom but delivers the soul to destruction.

sens: To become or be devoid of sharpness or point
To have worn, damaged, or sensitive teeth due to an unpleasant sensation
H6949.detail:
1. The word primarily describes a tool that has lost its effectiveness because its edge has become dull. In Ecclesiastes 10:10, iron is said to be "dull" when it has lost its sharpness: the worker must then "increase his strength" to accomplish his task because the tool no longer bites into wood or stone as it should.
2. In a figurative and more common sense in the Bible, the word denotes the unpleasant sensation felt in the teeth when biting into a sour or unripe grape: the teeth contract, tense up, as if they are losing their normal capacity. In Jeremiah 31:29-30 and Ezekiel 18:2, this phenomenon becomes an image of the transmission of guilt from one generation to another — the fathers eat sour grapes, and the children suffer the painful consequences in their teeth.
H6949.origine: The Hebrew verb derives from a root that expresses the idea of a decrease, a reduction in effectiveness or sensitivity. The image is that of a sharp edge becoming soft, a point becoming dull, or a sensation weakening or becoming bitter. The word thus paints very concrete realities: the lost sharpness, the suffering tooth.
H6949.emploi: The verb appears four times in the Old Testament. The first occurrence in Ecclesiastes 10:10 uses it in the literal sense: a dull iron forces the worker to exert more effort. Three other occurrences, in Jeremiah 31:29-30 and Ezekiel 18:2, use the sensory image of teeth: the fathers eating green grapes cause their children this annoying sensation in their teeth. This expression then becomes a proverbial formula in the Bible to illustrate the question of the relationship between the sins of the fathers and the responsibility of the children — a central theological debate in these passages.
H6949.portee: This word helps the reader grasp the difference between being responsible for one's personal actions and simply being affected by the consequences of another's sin. The image of irritated teeth reminds us that we can suffer from what others have done, but it does not mean that we are guilty of their actions — we remain responsible only for our own choices before God.

sens: To gather people in one place
To summon someone to an assembly
To gather a group for collective action
To come together (reflexive sense)
H6950.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: to physically gather people in the same place. In Exodus 32:1, the people "assemble" around Aaron in Moses' absence. It is a simple gathering of bodies in a common space.
2. The act of summoning: calling someone to present themselves at an assembly, often by an authority. In Numbers 10:7, the priest sounds the trumpet to "summon" the assembly of Israel. It is giving an order or a signal for people to gather.
3. To assemble for a common action: gathering a group for a specific purpose — war, judgment, religious act. In Esther 8:11, the king allows the Jews to "gather" and defend themselves together. In 1 Chronicles 15:3, David "assembles" all Israel for a solemn religious ceremony.
4. To come together spontaneously: when the subject gathers themselves without external summons. In Judges 20:1, all the children of Israel "gather" as one man before the Lord.
H6950.origine: The Hebrew root קָהַל (qa.hal) expresses the idea of gathering or assembling. It is related to the noun קָהָל (qa.hal), which means "assembly" or "congregation" — the group of people gathered together. In the biblical context, this verb often describes solemn moments when the people of Israel gather before God or to carry out an order.
H6950.emploi: The verb appears 39 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is used in various contexts: military (gathering before battle), religious (gathering for worship or festivals), judicial (gathering for decisions), and civil. Kings and religious authorities regularly "summon" the assembly: David in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 15:3), Solomon for the moving of the ark (1 Kings 8:1-2). Sometimes the people "gather" themselves in reaction to a crisis (Judges 20:1). The usage can be neutral or imply tension: in Numbers 16:3 and 16:19, the assembly "gathers" against Moses and Aaron in rebellion.
H6950.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of assembly in the religious life of Israel. For the Christian, it evokes the gathering of God's people around His Word and ordinances. It is also a call to gather with other believers, not by chance but with intention — to worship together, listen to God, and make common decisions. The verb emphasizes that faith is not solitary: it is lived and strengthened in the gathered community.
