sens: Group of people gathered together
The whole people of Israel summoned for a particular occasion
Large multitude, mass of people
Organized community of God's people
H6951.detail:
1. The word first designates a group of people gathered, whether called for an important decision, a war, or a religious ceremony — it is the idea of coming together. When Moses summons the people at the rock (Numbers 20:10), he gathers the entire assembly for a serious moment.
2. More broadly, it refers to the entirety of Israel itself understood as a united community, capable of receiving commandments or blessings together. King Solomon blesses "the whole assembly of Israel" (1 Kings 8:55) — it is the people as a body.
3. The word can also simply express a large multitude or a numerous crowd. Jeremiah speaks of a "multitude of great nations" coming against Babylon (Jeremiah 50:9): it is the image of an imposing mass.
4. In a religious context, the assembly becomes the organized people of God under His authority: a community that listens to the Law, participates in sacrifices, and forms one body before God.
H6951.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to call" or "to summon" — the assembly is first those who are called together. This same root gives rise to other words for "voice" and "cry." The starting image is that of the call that gathers: the assembly is summoned by raising the voice, sounding the trumpet. The word illustrates the idea that the people of Israel exist primarily when they are gathered, united by a common divine call.
H6951.emploi: The word appears 116 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the narratives of the Law (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy) and the history of the kings. It designates sometimes the assembly summoned at Sinai to receive the Ten Commandments (Deuteronomy 9:10), sometimes the crowd gathered to march to war (Numbers 22:4), and sometimes the entire people present for the great festivals (2 Chronicles 30:13). A recurring context is that the assembly must be excluded from the religious community if it has become impure (Leviticus 4:13-14). It is a term of great legal and religious force: the assembly is not limited to an informal crowd, it is the recognized people of God in its structure.
H6951.portee: This word reminds the reader that the people of God are never a collection of isolated individuals, but a community called to gather. When God blesses Abraham by promising a "multitude" (Genesis 28:3), He promises not only a numerous offspring but a united people. For the Christian, this evokes the image of the Church: the New Testament will apply the idea of assembly to the Christian community itself, called and gathered to worship God.

sens: Group of people gathered together
People or community gathered before God
Body of believers forming a community
H6952.detail:
1. In the most concrete sense, an assembly is a group of people gathered in the same place for a common reason. In Nehemiah 5:7, Nehemiah gathers a large "crowd" around the nobles and officials to reprimand them: it is a meeting called for judgment or collective decision.
2. In a religious context, the assembly refers to the people of God gathered, particularly in their moments of communion with the Lord. When Moses speaks in Deuteronomy 33:4 of the law as the "inheritance of the assembly of Jacob," he evokes the entire people of Israel united as a community under divine law.
3. The assembly can also evoke the idea of a permanent community, not just gathered temporarily, but forming a body united by a covenant or common commitment to God.
H6952.origine: The Hebrew word קְהִלָּה (qehillah) comes from the root קהל (qahal), which means "to gather" or "to call together." This root evokes the image of voices rising, of people being summoned. The word is used notably for the people of Israel when they are gathered before God, particularly at moments of covenant or revelation of His will.
H6952.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible provided. In Deuteronomy 33:4, it refers to the assembly of Jacob as the people receiving the Law — it is a solemn designation of the covenant people. In Nehemiah 5:7, it takes on a more practical meaning: a crowd gathered for public reprimand. The context shows that the assembly can be convened for the exercise of justice or authority within the community.
H6952.portee: For the believer, this word reminds them that they are not alone in their faith: they belong to an assembly, a people gathered by God. The notion of inheritance (Deuteronomy 33:4) invites us to see divine Law not as an individual burden, but as a communal good, received and carried together. It is an invitation to communal life and to just authority exercised within the body of God's people.

sens: one who speaks publicly before an assembly
one who gathers and utters words, maxims, teachings
one who proclaims or announces a message
H6953.detail:
1. The word primarily designates someone who speaks publicly: the preacher addresses an assembly, taking the floor before a group. This is the role of the wise one who shares his reflection in Ecclesiastes 1:1.
2. It also refers to one who collects, organizes, and utters wise words: in Ecclesiastes 12:10, we see the preacher who "seeks pleasant words" and "writes words of truth." His work is to gather wisdom and put it into form for teaching.
3. More broadly, it is one who proclaims a message before others, who serves as a spokesperson. The preacher does not just speak randomly: he has something to say, a weighed and structured word that he addresses to his audience.
H6953.origine: The Hebrew word קֹהֶלֶת (qohélet) comes from the root קהל (qahal) which means "to assemble, gather." The preacher is thus one who addresses a gathered assembly (qahal), or who gathers words. In Greek, this word became Ecclesiastes (Ekklésiast ès), which literally means "one who speaks in the assembly" (ekklèsia). The name of the book "Ecclesiastes" comes directly from this title.
H6953.emploi: This word is exclusively concentrated in the book of Ecclesiastes, which presents it as the title and function of the one who speaks: the wise one who reflects on life, work, pleasure, and death. It appears seven times, notably at the beginning (Ecclesiastes 1:1-2, 1:12) where the speaker identifies himself as the preacher, and at the end of the book (Ecclesiastes 12:10-12) where his work is described: he has "sought" good words, he has "written" them with uprightness, and his words are like "nails firmly driven." It is the only biblical book that carries this title as the central identity of the author.
H6953.portee: For the reader, this word invites them to take the word of the wise seriously. The preacher is not a idler who rambles: he is someone who has gathered, weighed, written, and organized his thoughts for his audience. Listening to the preacher is to open oneself to an honest reflection on the meaning of life, even if it raises difficult questions. Wisdom is best shared, and it speaks directly to those who hear it.

sens: A stop in the journey of the Israelites in the desert
H6954.detail: 1. Kehélatha is a place where the Israelites stopped during their long wandering in the desert, between the exodus from Egypt and the entry into Canaan. The name appears in the list of stops during their desert crossing (Numbers 33:22-23), where it simply marks a campsite among the forty that punctuate this forty-year journey.
H6954.origine: The name literally means "assembly" or "convocation" in Hebrew (from the root qhl, which speaks of the gathering of the people). It is a place name that reminds us that each stop in the desert was also a step in the communal life of the people of God, gathered around a common faith and vocation.
H6954.emploi: Kehélatha appears only twice in the Bible, both in chapter 33 of the Book of Numbers, which systematically enumerates the forty-two stops in the desert. It is located between Rissa (upstream) and the mountain of Schapher (downstream). This place has no other narrative or incident attached to it: it is mentioned only as a landmark in the journey of the people.
H6954.portee: This name reminds us that each step of our journey with God — even the passages that seem ordinary or desolate — is part of a journey that God knows every detail of and that brings us closer to His promise.

sens: Son of Levi and head of a Levitical family
Ancestor of the Kehathites, a branch of the Israelite priesthood
H6955.detail:
1. Kehath is a man of the tribe of Levi, son of Levi and brother of Gershon and Merari (Genesis 46:11). He lived during the time of Egypt and the desert, and he is the father of Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel (Numbers 3:19). Through his son Amram, he becomes the grandfather of Moses and Aaron, the two greatest leaders of Israel.

2. Kehath is the founder of one of the three major families of Levites: the Kehathites. This family receives sacred responsibilities in the sanctuary, notably the care of the most holy objects — the ark, the table, the lampstand, and the altar (Numbers 4:4). The Kehathites are also designated to receive Levitical cities as an inheritance (Joshua 21:26). His name, which means "assembly," reflects his role as the founder of a community.
H6955.origine: The name Kehath (קְהָת) means "assembly" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that evokes gathering and meeting. Kehath is the second of the three sons of Levi, from whom the Kehathites (קְהָתִים) descend, designated by the adjective Kehathite throughout the Old Testament. His lineage becomes one of the most prestigious in the Levitical priesthood.
H6955.emploi: Kehath is mentioned 29 times in the provided biblical texts, mainly in Numbers and Chronicles. He first appears in Genesis 46:11 during the descent into Egypt. His children are listed in Exodus 6:18 and Numbers 3:19. The passages in Numbers (3:17 to 4:15) describe the cultic duties of the Kehathites: they guard the most sacred objects of the sanctuary and transport them during the camp. The passages in Joshua enumerate the cities given to the Kehathite families in Canaan. Chronicles trace his complete genealogy and his role in the organization of worship, notably during the time of David (1 Chronicles 15:5 and 23:12).

sens: Descendant de Qéhat, fils de Lévi
Membre de la tribu de Lévi chargé de fonctions religieuses au tabernacle et au temple
H6956.detail:
1. A Kehathite is a descendant of Qehat, the second son of Levi (Numbers 26:57). Qehat himself had four sons: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel, from whom the four main families of the Kehathites descended.
2. The Kehathites formed an important branch of the Levites, with specific responsibilities in the service of the tabernacle and the temple. They guarded the most sacred objects of worship (Numbers 4:18), and they were counted separately during the censuses (Numbers 3:27). They lived in certain cities that had been assigned to them, notably in the territory of Judah (Joshua 21:10, 1 Chronicles 6:54).
H6956.origine: The word comes from Qehat (קְהָת), the name of Levi's son from whom this family derives. The suffix -i (-ִי) indicates belonging: "one who belongs to Qehat." The meaning of the name Qehat is not clearly established, but this family became one of the three major divisions of the priestly tribe of Levi.
H6956.emploi: The term appears 15 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the books of Numbers, Joshua, and 1-2 Chronicles. These usages concern the counting of the Kehathites (Numbers 3:27, 26:57), their functions at the tabernacle (Numbers 4:18, 4:37), the order of march in the desert (Numbers 10:21), and the allocation of the cities designated for them (Joshua 21:4, 21:10). In 2 Chronicles, they are also seen involved in the religious reforms of the temple (2 Chronicles 29:12, 34:12).

sens: Cordon ou fil tendu servant à mesurer ou à tracer une ligne droite
Répétition monotone et incompréhensible de paroles
H6957A.detail:
1. In a literal sense, a rule is a cord or string that is stretched to measure a distance or to draw a straight line. It is the tool of the mason or carpenter who wants to ensure that his wall or construction is aligned.
2. In Isaiah 28:10 and 28:13, God criticizes the leaders of Judah who refuse to truly listen to His word: they receive it as a succession of empty formulas, repeated endlessly — "line upon line, line upon line" — without ever understanding or obeying it. It is a word reduced to noise, to hollow chatter.
H6957A.origine: The Hebrew word קַו likely comes from a root that evokes the act of stretching or drawing. In Isaiah 28, it plays on the sound itself: the repeated words become onomatopoeic, imitating the sound of a lesson being recited without being digested, like a child mumbling a lesson without understanding it.
H6957A.emploi: The word appears twice, both in Isaiah 28:10 and 28:13, in the same oracle of judgment. God denounces the leaders (perhaps the priests) who claim to teach the people but only churn out empty, repetitive, and unintelligible formulas. The divine word, which should be a living and transformative revelation, is for them just an inert echo — as if one were listening to a lesson without understanding anything. This monotonous and sterile repetition symbolizes their stubborn refusal to welcome the true message of God.
H6957A.portee: This passage invites the believer to ask whether he is truly listening to the word of God or merely reciting formulas. True faith is not a mechanical repetition, but a living listening and obedience. God calls for an understanding of the heart, not a sterile accumulation of words.

sens: To gather, to assemble in one place
To expect, to rely on something or someone
To wait confidently for the fulfillment of a promise
H6960B.detail: 1. The primary meaning of the word is physical: the waters gather in one place during creation (Genesis 1:9). It conveys the idea of things coming together, concentrating in a unique location. 2. From this concrete sense arises a spiritual meaning: to hope means to gather inwardly towards someone or something, directing one's attention and trust forward. The islands "hope" in God (Isaiah 60:9), meaning their hearts and attention turn towards Him with expectation. 3. The word expresses an active, confident expectation: one does not remain passive; one expects God to act. When the nations gather in Jerusalem in the name of the Lord (Jeremiah 3:17), they collectively fulfill the hope of a restoration that God has promised.
H6960B.origine: The Hebrew root קָוָה (qavah) first refers to the idea of gathering, binding together dispersed things. It expresses the action of concentrating, focusing. Transitioning from the physical realm to the spiritual realm, the word has taken on the meaning of waiting or hoping: turning one's attention, heart, and faith towards something or someone in the future. This shift from the concrete to the figurative is common in ancient languages.
H6960B.emploi: This verb appears 3 times in the Bible, and its usages clearly demonstrate this transition from the concrete to the figurative. In Genesis 1:9, it describes the gathering of waters on the day of creation. In Isaiah 60:9 and Jeremiah 3:17, it expresses the confident expectation of the nations towards God and His future action. The three contexts reveal that gathering and hoping are two facets of the same word: to hope is to gather inwardly towards the one in whom we place our trust, concentrating our expectation towards a promised fulfillment.
H6960B.portee: This word teaches the reader that biblical hope is not a vague wish, but an active concentration of the heart towards God and His promises. To hope is to gather in Him, to fix our trust on the one who alone can accomplish what we await. It is an internal gesture of unity and direction.

sens: Feeling of repugnance, physical or moral aversion towards something or someone
Repugnance one feels towards oneself, one's own behavior
Hatred, abomination
Internal rejection of a behavior or reality
H6962.detail: 1. Disgust is primarily a spontaneous repugnance, a strong aversion: it is what God feels towards a people who refuse His ways despite forty years of evidence of His power (Psalms 95:10). It is also the believer's repulsion towards those who violate God's word (Psalms 119:158). 2. The word more strongly designates the disgust one conceives of oneself, a deep self-repugnance: it is when the sinner, becoming aware of his infamies, rejects himself with horror (Ezekiel 6:9, Ezekiel 20:43). 3. This feeling is akin to absolute hatred: in Psalms 139:21, the one who loves God feels disgust for his enemies, united with contempt. 4. Biblical disgust is always linked to a realization: the reminder of a sullied past provokes this repugnance towards oneself (Ezekiel 36:31), marking the turning point of conversion.
H6962.origine: The Hebrew verb קוּט (qut) expresses a visceral repugnance, an aversion of the heart and soul. Its root evokes something rejected, undesirable. In biblical Hebrew, the word is mainly used in the reflexive or passive form (Niphal and Hithpolel), as disgust is primarily an internal reaction: one does not perform disgust, one feels it. This verb is connected to the realm of visceral emotions of rejection and deep weariness.
H6962.emploi: The verb קוּט (qut) appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, always in a context of intense emotional or moral significance. In the Psalms, it first expresses God's reaction to Israel's unfaithfulness (Psalms 95:10) and to transgression (Psalms 119:158), then the believer's feeling towards God's enemies (Psalms 139:21). However, it is in the three passages from Ezekiel (6:9, 20:43, 36:31) that the word takes on its full spiritual force: it designates the repugnance of the exiled people towards their own idolatrous and sullied past. This self-condemnation, this rejection of oneself, marks the path to repentance and restoration. Disgust here becomes the sign that grace begins to act.
H6962.portee: This word teaches the believer that disgust towards evil is not a weakness, but the natural reaction of a conscience illuminated by God. Feeling disgust towards sin, especially towards one's own faults, is the beginning of true conversion (Ezekiel 36:31). It is when the sinner feels disgust for himself that he becomes capable of change: this repugnance towards evil is the door through which restorative grace enters.

sens: Sound produced by human speech or vocal emission
Noise, sound produced by an instrument or a natural phenomenon
Call or cry addressed to someone
Word, message, or order to listen to
Obedience or submission to an order, an authority
Reputation or public testimony
H6963A.detail:
1. The voice is primarily the sound of human speech: this is how Jacob recognizes Israel "by the voice," touching his hand to verify his identity (Genesis 27:22). It is the most direct vehicle of communication between people.
2. The word also designates any noise or sound: the voice of the blood crying from the ground (Genesis 4:10), the cry of the shepherds when God ravages their pastures (Jeremiah 25:36). It is the sonic image of a situation, of urgency.
3. A voice can be a call or a cry: when Abraham hears "the voice" of God calling him, then again telling him, "Do not lay a hand on the child" (Genesis 22:11), it is a divine word that directly addresses him.
4. To listen or obey the voice means to receive and follow an order or teaching: Saul claims to have "listened to the voice of the Lord" by following the path God indicated (1 Samuel 15:20). It is to make what is commanded one's own.
5. To obey someone's voice means to submit to their authority: God promises blessings and victories to those who listen to His voice (Deuteronomy 28:1-2), and curses to those who reject it (Deuteronomy 28:15).
6. The voice also becomes public testimony or reputation: it can cry out to God in demand for justice, or manifest the anger of the people.
H6963A.origine: The Hebrew word qol primarily designates sound, the sound wave as a physical phenomenon. Its basic image is that of a vibration that propagates and reaches the ear. Used for human voice, it encompasses both the raw sound and the meaning carried by the words. In the biblical context, "listening to the voice" of God becomes a major expression: it is more than hearing a noise; it is welcoming the divine word as an authority that imposes itself on the conscience and demands a response.
H6963A.emploi: The word qol appears more than 300 times in the Old Testament, present in all the narrative and wisdom books. It is very common in Genesis, Exodus, and Deuteronomy, where it often expresses obedience or refusal to obey the voice of God. In the narratives, it first designates direct human voice (Jacob recognized by his voice). In the laws and teachings, "listening to the voice" becomes synonymous with moral and religious obedience: obeying the voice of the prophet or priest, obeying the voice of the Lord. The psalms make it a motif of prayer: the psalmist asks that God "hear his voice" (Psalms 5:4). The meaning varies little: there is always communication, transmission of a message that awaits a response.
H6963A.portee: Understanding "the voice of God" transforms biblical reading: it is not an abstraction, but a concrete call that demands a concrete response. This invites the reader to listen actively, to distinguish between what comes from God and what comes from elsewhere (like Adam listening to the woman rather than God in Genesis 3:17). The voice also establishes a personal relationship: God speaks, and His creatures are called to hear and obey, not out of servile fear but out of recognition of His benevolent authority.

sens: quality of what is trivial, carefree, nonchalant
lack of seriousness or depth in behavior
frivolity, irresponsibility
H6963B.detail:
1. The word describes a moral lightness, a carefree attitude towards evil. In Jeremiah 3:9, Israel is reproached for its "shocking" lightness — that is, its shameless boldness and indifference in committing spiritual adultery: it has betrayed its covenant with the Lord as if it were of no importance, without shame or remorse.
2. This lightness stands in contrast to the seriousness required in the covenant relationship with God. Treating infidelity towards the Lord lightly is to ignore its severity and consequences.
H6963B.origine: The Hebrew word qol primarily denotes voice, sound — what is audible and manifest. The meaning of "lightness" or "frivolity" derives from the idea of a light word, without weight, spoken carelessly. It refers to an attitude that takes things lightly, speaking or acting without moral gravity.
H6963B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 3:9. The prophet uses it to describe Israel's sin — its infidelity towards the Lord committed with a carefree boldness, without fear or hesitation. It is a rare word, chosen to emphasize the scandal: not only has Israel sinned, but it has done so as if it were indifferent, which exacerbates its guilt.
H6963B.portee: This word highlights a particularly grave sin: to sin not out of weakness, but out of deliberate contempt and lightness of heart. It calls the believer to treat their covenant with God with the seriousness it deserves, and to never confuse the grace of the Lord with the permission to sin without fear or remorse.

sens: The voice of a person speaking or shouting
The sound of a thing, a natural phenomenon, or an event
The sound of a musical instrument
What is heard, made audible
The call or command of an authority
The word of God that calls out
H6963H.detail:
1. The voice is primarily the sound produced by the mouth of a person who speaks, shouts, or calls. It is the unique way each person makes themselves heard: "And they heard the voice of the Lord God" (Genesis 3:8) refers to the living and speaking presence of God in the garden.
2. The word also denotes any sound produced by a thing or phenomenon: "At the sound of their neighing, the whole earth trembles" (Jeremiah 8:16) speaks of the clamor of horses in battle, and "the sound of the wings of the creatures, striking one against the other" (Ezekiel 3:13) evokes natural or supernatural sounds.
3. It is the sound emitted by a musical instrument: "harps and lyres, whose sound was heard from afar" (Ezra 3:13) shows that the voice can be musical.
4. More broadly, it is what manifests, what is heard and becomes perceptible: "like the sound of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of fools" (Ecclesiastes 7:6) compares sound to laughter.
5. Sometimes the word carries the sense of command or authoritative word: one "hears the voice" of the one who commands or teaches.
6. In the spiritual context, it is the personal word of God that addresses His people and demands response and obedience.
H6963H.origine: The Hebrew word qol (קוֹל) comes from a root that fundamentally means "to sound," "to resonate." It primarily denotes any auditory phenomenon: noise, sound, voice. The family of the word includes the idea of vibration, of transmitting a sound wave. In the Bible, this word is very common because the voice is the primary means of communication: God speaks through His voice, and people make themselves heard through their cries or words. Unlike modern cultures, where sight predominates, the Bible emphasizes the importance of what is "heard."
H6963H.emploi: The word qol appears more than a hundred times in the Old Testament, across all literary genres: historical narratives, poetry, wisdom, prophecy. It denotes human, animal, or divine voice, and the noise of natural phenomena or those caused by humans. In Exodus 19:16-19, the noise accompanies the presence of God at Sinai. In Psalms, "the voice" is that of God commanding, comforting, or judging. In Ecclesiastes and Song of Solomon, it is a word from everyday life that evokes love or vanity. In Jeremiah, "to hear the voice" often means to obey the prophetic call. The word can also express impact or reach: "whose sound was heard from afar" (Ezra 3:13) indicates that the voice or noise has a power of transmission.
H6963H.portee: Understanding the word "voice" opens the eyes of the Christian reader to the reality of divine communication: God does not speak primarily in writing, but through His living and personal word. When the text says "listen to the voice of the Lord," it invites active and conscious obedience, not passive. It is also a call to recognize that what is heard can come from God or the world, from wisdom or vanity — hence the importance of discerning "which voice" one listens to.

sens: Loud and resounding noise that accompanies lightning during a storm
Sound of the human voice or of an instrument
Expression of God's power manifested in nature
H6963I.detail:
1. Thunder is the crashing noise that accompanies lightning during a storm. It is an impressive and terrifying natural phenomenon, as seen during the plagues of Egypt: "The Lord sent thunder and hail" (Exodus 9:23). The Hebrew word qol denotes this powerful rumbling from the sky.
2. More broadly, qol means any distinct sound or noise: the voice of a person speaking, or the sound of a musical instrument. In Exodus 19:19, Moses hears the voice of God responding to him: "Moses spoke, and God answered him with a loud voice."
3. In the Bible, thunder becomes a sign of divine power. God commands the thunders just as He commands the rain and lightning, showing His absolute authority over creation. Samuel calls upon the Lord to send thunder and rain, so that the people recognize God's presence and strength (1 Samuel 12:17).
H6963I.origine: The Hebrew word qol primarily means "voice" or "sound" in general. It is not a specialized word: it denotes any noise that is heard, from a whisper to a clamor. Thunder is a spectacular and divine manifestation of this. The same root has given rise in Hebrew to several words related to sound and voice. In Greek, the words ἦχος (êchos) and φωνή (phônè) capture this wide range of meanings.
H6963I.emploi: The word qol appears 13 times in the provided biblical passages, mainly to denote thunder during the plagues of Egypt (Exodus 9:23, 28, 29, 33, 34) and during the theophany at Sinai (Exodus 19:16, 19; 20:18). It also occurs when Samuel asks God to send thunder as a sign of His power (1 Samuel 12:17, 18). Job mentions thunder as a manifestation of divine wisdom governing meteorology (Job 28:26; 38:25). Only once, in Exodus 19:19, does the word clearly refer to the voice of God speaking to Moses. Everywhere else in this collection, it is thunder that dominates: qol is the means by which God reminds humanity of His sovereign domain over nature.
H6963I.portee: Thunder in the Bible is never a neutral phenomenon: it is the voice of God speaking through the elements. When God sends thunder, He manifests His power and demands obedience. For the Christian, this reminds us that God is not distant, but active in the visible world. Thunder helps us understand that His power cannot be ignored and that His authority extends over all creation.

sens: Sound produced by the speech or cry of a person
Sound produced by a musical instrument
Noise, any sound
Message, word addressed to someone
Proclamation, public announcement
Obedience to an order or request
H6963J.detail:
1. The voice is primarily the sound produced by someone when they speak or cry. It is the natural means of communication: one listens to someone's voice to hear what they say (1 Samuel 28:21: the woman says to Saul, "your servant has listened to your voice").
2. The word also refers to the sound produced by an instrument, such as a trumpet or a harp during a religious service.
3. More broadly, it encompasses any noise, any sound: in Genesis 45:16, the "noise" of the arrival of Joseph's brothers spreads throughout Pharaoh's palace.
4. The voice becomes the vector of the message itself: to obey someone's voice is to obey their order (2 Kings 10:6: "if you obey my voice").
5. When one "publishes" a proclamation, they "make heard" an official voice in the community: in Exodus 36:6, Moses "proclaims" in the camp that no one should bring additional offerings.
6. In this extension, "to obey the voice" means to submit to what is commanded or requested.
H6963J.origine: The Hebrew word qol paints the image of sound that spreads and is heard. It comes from an ancient root common to several Semitic languages. The word initially evokes the physical sensation of noise, then naturally extends to the meaning of message and authority expressed through speech. In the Greek Bible, it is often translated as phonè, which has the same range of meaning.
H6963J.emploi: This word appears 13 times in the provided references, mainly in the Old Testament. It is used to describe a voice that is listened to (Exodus 4:8, 1 Samuel 28:21, 2 Kings 10:6), a noise that spreads (Genesis 45:16), and a public proclamation (Exodus 36:6, 2 Chronicles 24:9, 2 Chronicles 30:5). Its meaning shifts from physical sound to message, then to the authority expressed by that message: to obey the voice is primarily to listen, but also to submit to the heard order. The context always determines whether one is speaking of the sound itself or its content.
H6963J.portee: Understanding the biblical voice means grasping how God communicates with His people and how authority is exercised within a community. When God speaks through His voice or when one is urged to obey a voice (that of a king, a prophet), it is always a matter of obedient listening. The Christian discovers that the voice calls for a decision: one cannot simply hear without choosing to submit or refuse.

sens: What comes out of the mouth to communicate: the word, the speech
The sound produced by something: noise, tone
The echo that spreads, what is heard from afar
The expression of a will or a feeling
H6963K.detail:
1. The voice is primarily the living word that comes out of the mouth to be heard and understood. When Moses says to the Israelites, "If they do not believe you at the voice of the first sign" (Exodus 4:8), he is speaking of the word he will address, the message he will proclaim. It is the voice as a means of communication, of transmitting an intelligible word.
2. The word also designates the sound, the noise produced by any object or instrument. In 2 Chronicles 5:13, the trumpets and cymbals "sound," meaning they emit their voice, their own tone. Anything that vibrates and produces sound has its voice.
3. The voice is what is heard, what reaches the ear even from afar. When "the Lord heard the noise of your words" (Deuteronomy 1:34), this voice traveled through space; it resonated to Him. It is the sound as it spreads and is perceived.
4. Finally, the voice carries an intention, a will, an emotion. To listen to someone is to recognize their authority, to accept their message. The voice becomes the visible sign of a presence and an acting power.
H6963K.origine: The Hebrew word qol comes from a root that expresses the idea of vibration and sound propagation. It is a very ancient word, probably onomatopoeic in origin: it directly evokes noise, the sound that spreads. Ancient Greek often translates this word as "phonè" (φωνή), which also means voice and sound. Throughout the Bible, qol designates what is heard, from the voice of God speaking to the cry of animals.
H6963K.emploi: The word qol appears more than 400 times in the Old Testament. It describes the human voice when speaking or crying, the voice of God communicating with His people, the noise of musical instruments, thunder, and many other sounds. In Exodus 4:8, it is the word of the sign that was not heard the first time. In Deuteronomy 1:34 and 5:28, it is the murmured or proclaimed words that God perceives. In 2 Chronicles 5:13, the instruments "make their voice sound." The word easily shifts from physical sound to a meaningful message because the voice always communicates something.
H6963K.portee: For the believer, understanding that God has a "voice" and that He "listens" to our voice means that the relationship with Him is alive and personal. It is not an abstract force, but someone who speaks, who makes Himself heard, and who hears our words. When the Bible says "listen to the voice of the Lord," it invites to a voluntary obedience, to the reception of a message. Recognizing the voice of God is to recognize Him as present and alive.

sens: Sound produced by a person's speech
Noise or sound produced by any source
The expression of speech or cry, as a bearer of meaning or intention
Listening, attention to what is said
H6963L.detail:
1. The voice is primarily the sound produced by a person when they speak: it is by their voice that one recognizes someone, that one hears their words. In 1 Samuel 28:22, the woman asks the king to listen to her: "Listen now, you too, to the voice of your servant," meaning her words, her call.
2. The word can refer to any noise or sound: in 2 Kings 7:10, the lepers note that in the camp of the Syrians, "there is no voice of man," meaning no noise, no sound of human presence — tied horses, tied donkeys, empty tents.
3. The voice often carries an intention, a cry, a call: it is not just a simple sound, but the expression of what one wants to communicate, say, or request. That is why one "listens to the voice" of someone — it is to obey, to respond to their call.
4. Sometimes "voice" means the act of listening itself: one speaks of "giving voice to" or "listening to the voice" to mean "paying attention to what is said."
H6963L.origine: The Hebrew word קוֹל (qol) comes from a very ancient root that designates noise, sound, everything that is heard. It shares the same root as words in ancient Arabic and other Semitic languages. The initial image is that of something resonating, striking the ear. In Greek, this word was often translated as φωνή (phôné), which has the same scope: voice or noise.
H6963L.emploi: The word קוֹל appears very frequently in the Hebrew Bible, in all genres of texts. Here, it is used three times in very different contexts: in 1 Samuel 28:22, it is the voice of a servant imploring the king; in 2 Samuel 13:14, it is probably a cry or a word; in 2 Kings 7:10, it is the absence of human noise in the camp. The word can thus designate both a personal call, a clamor, or simply the absence of sound — it encompasses all noises and all calls that can be heard.
H6963L.portee: The voice, in the Bible, is the means by which God and man speak to each other. To listen to someone's voice is to pay attention to their words and obey them. This word reminds us that the word is alive: it is not written, it resonates, it demands a response. For the reader, this emphasizes the importance of hearing and obeying what is said to us — whether it be the voice of a servant, that of a parent, or that of God Himself.

sens: Benjamite of Jerusalem after the exile
H6964G.detail: Kolaja is an ancestor mentioned in the genealogy of Sallu, who settled in Jerusalem after the return from Babylonian captivity. His name appears only once in the Bible, in the list of the inhabitants of Jerusalem under Nehemiah's governance (Nehemiah 11:7). He is the son of Maaséja and the father of Pedaja, belonging to the tribe of Benjamin.
H6964G.origine: The name Kolaja means "voice of Jehovah" in Hebrew, formed from "kol" (voice) and a theophoric element referring to the Lord. It is a typical theophoric name of the time, expressing a relationship with God. Although it carries a rich meaning, this character is known only through this brief genealogical mention.
H6964G.emploi: Kolaja is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:7, in a genealogical list of Benjamites who returned from exile in Babylon. He appears as a link in the genealogical chain leading back to Sallu, one of the notable figures who resettled in Jerusalem. This mention anchors the story of the post-exilic restoration by showing that the Benjaminite families regained their footing in the holy city.

sens: father of the false prophet Ahab during the divided monarchy
H6964H.detail: Kolaja is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the prophet Jeremiah denounces the false prophets. He is the father of Ahab, a man who claimed to speak in God's name but prophesied lies (Jeremiah 29:21). God promises that he and his companion Zedekiah will be delivered to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and will perish before the eyes of the exiles. Kolaja thus represents a family involved in religious deception in Jerusalem.
H6964H.origine: The name Kolaja means "voice of the Eternal" in Hebrew (from "qol", voice, and "Yah", abbreviated divine name). It is a theophoric name, meaning it incorporates the name of God. The contrast is striking: despite this name that evokes divine speech, Kolaja's son will be a false prophet who contradicts the true word of the Eternal.
H6964H.emploi: Kolaja appears only once in Scripture, in Jeremiah 29:21. The context is that of the Babylonian exile: Jeremiah writes to the exiles to warn them against the false prophets who deceive them by claiming that the captivity will be brief. Ahab, son of Kolaja, is one of these impostors. His name disappears after this verse, but his story illustrates divine judgment on those who counterfeit the word of the Lord and deceive the people in God's name.
H6964H.portee: This account warns believers to remain vigilant against false prophets and deceptive teachers who present themselves in God's name. The example of Kolaja and his son reminds us that even a name that honors the Lord does not guarantee faithfulness; only the fruits and alignment with true divine revelation matter. It is a lesson in spiritual discernment for all times.

sens: The adversary, one who opposes (possessive form: my adversary)
In a collective sense: a hostile people or group
H6965A.detail:
1. The word expresses the idea of direct opposition, personal resistance. In Jeremiah 51:1, it refers to the enemies of Babylon, those who threaten and fight against it.
2. When used in the collective sense, "against me" designates not a single opponent, but a group of people united against a common target — here, the hostile peoples against Babylon who form a collective force of opposition.
H6965A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of rising up, opposing, standing against. The possessive form "-kamai" (my adversary, those against me) shows that the opposition is viewed from the perspective of the one who suffers it. This term fits within the biblical vocabulary of struggle and conflict.
H6965A.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 51:1, where the prophet announces judgment against Babylon. It is used to designate the enemy that stands against the city of Babylon and will be the instrument of divine punishment. In this context, God himself raises up the one who opposes Babylon, showing that the judgment comes from Him.
H6965A.portee: This word reminds us that in God's plan, even those who rise against the powerful of this world are instruments in the hands of the Lord. It invites the believer to see beyond the appearances of human conflict to discern the hand of God that judges.

sens: to stand up, to get up (of the body)
to depart, to set out
to rise against someone, to attack
to surge, to appear, to emerge
to be established, confirmed, durable
to accomplish, to realize, to implement
H6965B.detail:
1. To stand up, to get up: the movement of the body transitioning from a sitting or lying position to a vertical position. "She rose, she and her daughters-in-law" (Ruth 1:6): this is primarily a simple physical gesture, getting up to act.

2. To depart, to set out: "She rose […] to leave the land of Moab" (Ruth 1:6); "they rose and went each their own way" (1 Kings 1:49). The verb describes the initial momentum, the moment one begins to move to depart.

3. To rise against, to attack: "Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him" (Genesis 4:8); "It is a people that rises like a lioness" (Numbers 23:24). Here the verb carries a hostile or combative nuance.

4. To surge, to appear, to take shape: an event, a situation, a person that "rises" on the world stage, like a new king after the death of the previous one (Exodus 1:8).

5. To be established, confirmed, durable: "Be established and remain" expresses the idea that a promise, a covenant, or a reign "rises" and remains firm, unshakeable.

6. To accomplish, to realize: when God "raises" His word or His covenant, He puts them into action, making them active and effective in history.
H6965B.origine: An ancient and common Hebrew root, imagery of the body straightening up, of weight being lifted. The root also evokes the idea of stability and permanence: what rises and stands firm. It is used in all the main verbal forms in Hebrew (Qal, Piel, Hiphil), each adding a nuance: the Qal is the simple sense (to rise), the Hiphil reinforces (to cause to rise, to erect, to establish), the Piel adds the idea of accomplishment (to realize, to confirm).
H6965B.emploi: This verb appears about 370 times in the Hebrew text provided by the Segond 1910, especially in Genesis and Numbers. It is the fundamental verb of movement and action: patriarchs who rise to act (Abraham, Jacob, Moses), peoples who rise to fight, kings who emerge. Its primary meaning (to stand up) is the most frequent; the meaning "to depart" is very common in travel narratives. Gradually, the verb takes on more abstract meanings: "to be established" (a covenant), "to be confirmed" (a divine word), "to be accomplished" (a promise). In the later books (Ecclesiastes), the meaning becomes concrete again: "one rises at the sound of the bird" (Ecclesiastes 12:6).
H6965B.portee: For the believer, this verb is rich in spiritual meaning without forcing the text. To rise is to respond to God's call, to take action, not to remain passive. When God "raises" His promise or His king, it is because He is acting in history. And when He tells His people "rise up", it is a call to walk in faith, to stand against evil, to move toward the land He promises.

sens: To stand up, to rise after having lain down or fallen
To rise, to appear, to take action (in a physical or political sense)
To establish, to build, to set up a structure or an altar
To raise someone for a mission or a function
To stand firm, to endure, to remain valid
To fulfill, to accomplish, to implement a word or a promise
H6965H.detail:
1. To stand up, to rise after having lain down or fallen: this is the movement of the body transitioning from horizontal to vertical. Ecclesiastes 4:10 mentions one who falls and has no one to lift him up.
2. To rise, to appear, to take action in a political or hostile sense: this is when a power, a nation, or an adversary suddenly emerges and manifests. Habakkuk 1:6 speaks of the Chaldeans rising suddenly as a threat.
3. To establish, to build, to set up a structure or a sacred place: this is to physically erect or raise. Exodus 26:30 commands to set up the tabernacle according to the divine pattern; Numbers 7:1 recounts how Moses set up the tabernacle and consecrated it.
4. To raise someone for a special mission or function: this is to bring forth a person in history to accomplish God's work. Judges 2:16: the Lord raised judges to deliver Israel; 1 Samuel 2:8 says that God lifts the poor from the dust and places him among princes.
5. To stand firm, to endure, to remain in force or valid: this refers to what persists and does not collapse. Psalms 41:11 speaks of one who "rises" in strength against his enemies, and Isaiah 14:9 causes the shades to rise from their thrones.
6. To fulfill, to accomplish, to implement a word or a promise: this is to move a decision from plan to action. Hosea 6:2 promises that God will raise us up on the third day.
H6965H.origine: The root קוּם (qum) expresses the idea of verticality, stability, and permanence. It primarily describes the movement of standing up, and by extension, everything that is established, persists, and comes to fruition. It is an active and dynamic root, very frequent in biblical Hebrew, generating many derivatives (nouns, adjectives) related to establishment and consistency. The verb can take different forms that nuance the meaning: the simple form (Qal) primarily means "to rise"; the intensive form (Piel) emphasizes the idea of "to make stand" or "to accomplish"; the causative form (Hiphil) adds the idea of making arise or establishing by authority.
H6965H.emploi: This verb appears 37 times in the provided biblical usages, totaling about 90 times in the Old Testament, particularly in historical narratives (Exodus, Numbers, Judges, Samuel, Kings) and prophetic texts (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, Habakkuk). In passages related to worship, it denotes the erection of the tabernacle and altars (Exodus 26:30, Numbers 7:1, 2 Samuel 24:18). In narratives of deliverance and governance, it refers to the raising of judges or leaders (Judges 2:16, 1 Samuel 2:8). In prophetic contexts, it speaks of the rise of enemy powers (Habakkuk 1:6) or future resurrection (Hosea 6:2). The word can thus oscillate between the concrete (erecting a building) and the abstract (fulfilling a promise or raising a leader), but it always carries the idea of manifestation, establishment, or putting into action.
H6965H.portee: This verb reminds us that God does not abandon Israel: He raises deliverers, establishes His sanctuary among His people, and keeps His promises. For the believer, "to rise" is not just a physical act: it is also to respond to God's call, to rise after a moral fall, and to trust that God will fulfill His word. The promise of Hosea 6:2 about being raised on the third day also speaks, for the Church, of the certainty of resurrection in God's intention.

sens: To stand up, to rise physically
To rise against someone, to oppose
To emerge, to appear, to gain importance
To be established, to be confirmed, to remain valid
To set up, to erect, to build
To raise, to bring forth, to accomplish
H6965I.detail:
1. To rise: to stand on one's feet. This is the simplest physical movement — one thinks of someone getting up from their seat or bed. In Jeremiah 23:4, God says, "I will raise up shepherds over them" in Hebrew using the same verb, meaning "to set up."
2. To rise against: to emerge with hostile intent, to oppose. This is a military or conflictual use of the verb.
3. To emerge or become powerful: the word also carries the idea of something that begins to exist, that emerges on the public or political scene, and gains strength.
4. To be established, confirmed, valid: here the verb describes what persists, what remains firm. Numbers 30:12 speaks of "valid" vows — that is, they stand firm, unannulled. The same goes for a covenant that is "established": it stands, it endures.
5. To set up, to erect, to build: one erects an altar, a monument, an image (Judges 18:30). The verb here means to make something durable, based on solid foundations.
6. To raise, to bring forth, to accomplish: God "establishes" a covenant (Genesis 6:18), meaning He puts it into effect, realizes it, confirms it. This includes bringing forth a descendant destined for a role: "I will raise up your offspring" means "I will give you a son who will continue your lineage."
H6965I.origine: The verb comes from a root that paints the initial image of something that stands, that is upright and firm. The root qûm is very ancient in Hebrew and appears in related Semitic languages. It is the source of words like qômâ (stature, height) and qawwôm (that which stands upright). The verb has several forms depending on the context: simple (I rise), intensive (I set something up), causative (I make rise). This flexibility shows the deep connection between physical movement and the idea of establishing, making stable, and durable.
H6965I.emploi: The verb "to rise" (קוּם) is one of the most frequent in the Old Testament: 159 attestations here, spread across almost all historical books, in the prophets and wisdom literature. Beyond the physical sense (to rise from bed, to rise in assembly), it becomes a key theological verb: to establish a covenant, to fulfill a promise, to raise a prophet or a king. Genesis 6:18 opens this register with the covenant with Noah. The books of the Law (Deuteronomy, Leviticus, Numbers) imbue it with legal and cultic meaning — valid vows, established laws, witnesses setting up a cairn. The royal books describe it concerning dynasties and restorations of worship. Its usage oscillates between human action (to rise, to set up an altar, to build) and divine action (to establish a covenant, to raise a Messiah), unified by the idea that what stands persists and asserts itself.
H6965I.portee: This verb invites meditation on stability and validity. God who "establishes" His covenant does not let it collapse: He sets it like a house on durable foundations. For the believer, it is a promise of reliability. Likewise, "to rise" in assembly to testify (Job 30:28) or before an injustice refers to civil courage. Finally, the notion that God "raises" men for a purpose — a prophet, a king — teaches that history is not chaos: it is guided by the One who establishes kings and fulfills His words.

sens: One who opposes, attacks, or stands against someone
One who rises up in arms, revolts, or rebels
One who pursues in court, accuses, or testifies against someone
One who acts with hostility, malice, or violence
H6965J.detail:
1. An adversary is primarily someone who stands against you, who takes a position against you. It conveys the idea of rising up to oppose. In Exodus 15:7, after the victory at the Red Sea, the text speaks of those who rose up against Israel: it is the image of a warrior standing firm against his enemy.

2. The word more specifically designates one who attacks or pursues you in combat. In Deuteronomy 28:7, God promises to give Israel victory over its adversaries who will rise against it. It is the adversary in the warrior sense: one who stands armed.

3. An adversary can also be one who accuses or pursues you in court. In Job 16:8, the thinness of the righteous "rises up" against him like an adversary testifying in court: this is the judicial image of the word. In Psalms 27:12, it speaks of false witnesses who become adversaries.

4. More broadly, it refers to anyone who shows you hostility or hatred. In Psalms 92:12, the author speaks of his "wicked adversaries": the word captures the idea of someone who opposes you with malice.
H6965J.origine: The Hebrew verb קוּם (qum) fundamentally means "to rise" or "to stand up." From this basic idea naturally arises the concept of "to oppose" or "to attack": one who rises stands against you. The word has generated many derivatives in Hebrew to express establishment, confirmation, or fulfillment (like when something "rises" to become reality). In Greek, this verb is often translated as ἀνίστημι (anistémi), which carries the same image of rising and standing up.
H6965J.emploi: This word appears about 33 times in the provided passages, mainly in the Psalms and historical narratives. It is almost always used in the sense of adversary or enemy, particularly in contexts of conflict or persecution. Exodus 15:7 and Deuteronomy 28:7 use it for Israel's military enemies. The Psalms use it to describe those who persecute the righteous (Psalms 27:12, Psalms 92:12, Psalms 3:2). In 2 Samuel 18:31 and 18:32, we see how one who rises (the rebellious adversary) can also be defeated. The word also appears in contexts of legal accusation (Job 16:8, Job 20:27) where the adversary is one who testifies against you. Its meaning remains consistent: it always designates one who stands up, who rises against oneself.
H6965J.portee: This word sheds light for the believer on the experience of opposition and persecution. The Bible states plainly: there will be adversaries. But it also teaches that God sees these adversaries and can defeat or neutralize them. The Psalms, full of this word, show how the righteous can cry out to God in the face of their adversaries and obtain His protection. It is a call to recognize our true battles and to seek God for our defense, rather than relying on our own strength.

sens: To stand up, take position
To surge, appear, come into view
To stand against someone, to revolt
To establish firmly, to hold fast, to persist
To be set in place, to be established or confirmed
H6965K.detail:
1. To stand up, take position: the simplest and most concrete meaning. It is simply to rise from the ground or from a seat — like a person who gets up from a chair, or a guard who takes their post. In Judges 7:19, they "placed" (literally "raised") the guards around the camp: they took their position as sentinels.

2. To surge, appear, come into view: when something or someone "rises" to become visible or active. It is the image of the sun rising, or a person stepping out of the shadows to act in broad daylight.

3. To stand against someone, to revolt: the verb can evoke opposition or hostility. Someone rises *against* another — a posture of confrontation or rebellion.

4. To establish firmly, to hold fast, to persist: the word can mean "to remain standing" in a moral or spiritual sense — to be stable, solid, unshakeable. A promise that "rises" (or "holds") is a confirmed promise that does not waver.

5. To be set in place, to be established or confirmed: in certain contexts, it is the action of someone else who "raises" or "establishes" something — erecting a monument, instituting a law, fulfilling a given word.
H6965K.origine: The Hebrew verb קוּם comes from a very ancient root that images the action of standing upright. In Hebrew, there is also the noun קָם ("standing"), or the idea of permanence and stability. The word resonates with other Semitic languages: one thinks of the Arabic "qâma" (to stand). This root evokes the deep idea that what "rises" and "stands" is what is true, established, and enduring.
H6965K.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Old Testament. It appears in very varied contexts: raising an army, getting up from bed, rising to go somewhere, or rising in opposition. In the usage of Judges 7:19, the verb in the sense of "placing" or "establishing" guards shows how קוּם can mean "putting someone in their post." The meaning slightly changes according to the grammatical form (Qal, Hiphil, Piel): in Qal, it is mainly the subject who rises themselves; in Hiphil, it is someone else who raises or establishes them. The word also enriches itself with a very theological meaning: "to fulfill" a promise or "to stand firm" in the face of obstacles.
H6965K.portee: For the Christian reader, this verb reveals that stability and continuity come from God. When God "rises," it is to act and save. When His promises "rise" or "hold," it is the guarantee that His word will not fail. Conversely, understanding how man "rises" in opposition or rebellion shows the stakes of the choice to stand with God or against Him.

sens: To stand on one's feet, to leave a horizontal or seated position
To begin to act, to get moving after inaction
To appear, to emerge, to come into existence
To establish oneself, to take a stable and lasting position
To be set up, constituted, or established (for a thing)
H6966G.detail:
1. To stand on one's feet, to leave a horizontal or seated position: this is the physical movement of someone who rises. To King Nebuchadnezzar who sees men walking in the fire, "King Nebuchadnezzar was astonished, and he rose quickly" (Daniel 3:24): he leaves his seated or lying position to act.
2. To begin to act, to get moving after inaction: this is moving from immobility to action. "Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, and Joshua, son of Jehozadak, rose and began to build the house of God" (Ezra 5:2): they move out of their passivity to undertake the work.
3. To appear, to emerge, to come into existence: the word describes something that manifests on the scene. "After you, another kingdom will arise" (Daniel 2:39): a new power emerges, takes its place among the other kingdoms.
4. To establish oneself, to take a stable and lasting position: this is to stand firm, to persist. "These four great beasts are four kings who will arise from the earth" (Daniel 7:17): the kingdoms are constituted and persist.
5. To be set up, constituted, or established (for a thing): when the subject is passive, it expresses establishment or erection. The verb can also mean "to erect," "to raise" something (in its uses where it takes an object complement).
H6966G.origine: The Hebrew word קוּם (qum) comes from an ancient root denoting the action of standing up, of rising. The word family includes various forms: the simple form (Peal) means "to rise, to stand"; the intensive form (Pael) means "to establish, to erect"; the causative form (Aphel) means "to cause to rise, to establish." The basic image is that of the body rising, the vertical position asserting itself, an image that then extends to the idea of establishment, continuity, and even emergence or appearance.
H6966G.emploi: The verb קוּם appears 7 times in these biblical uses, especially in the book of Daniel and in Ezra. In Ezra 5:2, it describes the action of rising to undertake a task: Zerubbabel and Joshua "rise" to rebuild the Temple. In Daniel, the verb often has a broader meaning: it designates the emergence of future kingdoms (Daniel 2:39, 7:17), the action of rising at the right moment (Daniel 3:24, 6:19: the king rises from his bed), or the command addressed to a symbolic creature (Daniel 7:5: "Rise, eat"). The fundamental meaning remains the transition from rest to action, or from non-existence to existence.
H6966G.portee: This word speaks of the transition to action, the responsibility to rise to accomplish what is entrusted to us. For a believer, "to rise" is to come out of inertia, to respond to God's call, to undertake what He asks, like Zerubbabel and Joshua who rise to build the Temple despite obstacles. It is also an image of God's power, which establishes kingdoms and reigns according to His sovereign will.

sens: To rise, to assume a vertical position
To subsist, to persevere in a situation
To intervene, to act after inaction
To be established, constituted in function or authority
H6966H.detail:
1. To rise, to assume a vertical position: the action of moving from sitting or lying down to standing, or simply being in this posture. In Daniel 7:5, the bear "stood" on one side: the image is that of a beast planted on its paws, in a position of strength and threat.
2. To subsist, to persevere in a situation: to remain firm, to endure in a state or condition. This is less about the movement of rising than about the stability achieved.
3. To intervene, to act after inaction: to come out of immobility or inaction to act, to appear on the scene. The word evokes the idea of getting into motion to accomplish something.
4. To be established, constituted in function or authority: in the causative sense ("to be set up"), the verb means to be placed, constituted, designated for a lasting charge or role.
H6966H.origine: This Aramaic verb comes from a very ancient root that expresses the idea of station, stability, erection. It is common in Semitic: the Hebrew קוּם (qum) carries the same meaning. The basic image is that of the human or animal body moving to verticality, hence the extension to the idea of duration, firmness, and establishment. The causative forms (Pael, Aphel) reinforce this notion: one who "causes to stand" establishes, founds, institutes.
H6966H.emploi: This verb appears only once in this passage of biblical Aramaic. Daniel 7:5 uses it to describe the posture of the bear in the prophetic vision: the beast "stood" on one side, an image of an animal power planted, threatening, ready for action. The visionary context gives the word its strength: it is not a simple act of rising, but the establishment of a dominant and conquering presence. The verb in biblical Aramaic often carries a nuance of lasting establishment and authority.
H6966H.portee: For the reader, this word invites meditation on the spiritual posture: to stand firm in faith, to subsist firmly despite assaults, to be established by God in a mission. In the context of Daniel 7, the bear that "stands" reminds us that the powers of this world, even terrifying, exist only by divine permission and within the limits of His plan.

sens: To stand up, to physically elevate
To endure, persist, remain stable
To appoint, establish someone in a role
To set, put in place something (statue, rule, etc.)
To occur, intervene in history
H6966I.detail:
1. To stand up or physically elevate: the word primarily describes a bodily action, that of rising or raising something into the air. In Daniel 3:3, the statue that King Nebuchadnezzar 'raised' is an object erected to be worshiped: it is the image of something placed in a vertical and visible position.

2. To endure, persist, remain stable: beyond movement, the verb expresses solidity and permanence. The kingdom that God will raise 'will endure forever' (Daniel 2:44): it will not collapse, it will stand firm and last.

3. To appoint someone in a role: to establish a person means to constitute them in authority. King Nebuchadnezzar 'appointed' Daniel as chief of the magicians (Daniel 5:11): he places him at the head of a group, conferring this role upon him.

4. To set, put in place something, a rule or a reality: to issue an edict, a law, a decree. In Daniel 6:7-8, the officials request that an edict be 'established' with a severe prohibition: the rule is set, unchangeable, like something erected that cannot be brought down.

5. To occur, intervene in the course of history: the verb can also mean 'to come onto the scene', 'to manifest'. God will raise (lift) a kingdom that will oppose others (Daniel 2:44).
H6966I.origine: The word comes from a simple Semitic root that paints the image of rising or standing upright. In biblical Aramaic (the language of Daniel and Ezra), this verb has several forms: the simple form (P'al) means 'to rise, to stand'; the intensive form (Pael) reinforces the idea of 'establishing, appointing'; the causative form (Aphel) adds the idea of causing to rise or erect. The central image is always that of vertical position, stability, and solidity.
H6966I.emploi: This verb appears 23 times in the provided biblical usages, almost exclusively in Ezra and Daniel, that is, in the Aramaic texts of the Bible. In Ezra 6:18, it refers to appointing priests according to a given order. In Daniel, the word recurs constantly: it describes the erection of the statue (Daniel 3), the kings and kingdoms that rise one after another (Daniel 7), the appointment of governors and satraps by the king (Daniel 6), and especially the promise of God's kingdom that 'will endure' forever (Daniel 2:44). The context oscillates between administrative action (naming, establishing an order) and historical or divine action (a kingdom that arises or endures). The meaning nuances according to the object: with a person, it is to name; with a material thing, it is to erect; with a reality or a reign, it is to institute or ensure permanence.
H6966I.portee: This verb speaks to the believer about the solidity of what comes from God. When the text promises that the divine kingdom 'will endure forever', it uses this word to affirm that, unlike human empires that collapse, God's purpose will stand firm and will never waver. It is a word of confidence in the face of the changes and collapses of the world: God establishes what cannot be destroyed.

sens: Vertical dimension of an object, measured from bottom to top
Stature, height of a person's body
Degree of elevation or greatness, often with a nuance of pride or power
H6967.detail:
1. Height is the measurable vertical dimension of an object — in cubits for the constructions of the temple or Noah's ark. In Genesis 6:15, God prescribes an ark of thirty cubits in height; in Exodus 37:10, the acacia table has a height of one and a half cubits. It is simply a concrete measurement.
2. Height also refers to a person's stature, their physical size. In 1 Samuel 16:7, God sees beyond outward height: 'The Lord does not look at what man looks at; man looks at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart.' It is the bodily dimension of a person.
3. Height can evoke elevation or greatness, often with a connotation of power or pride. The trees in Ezekiel 31 are described by their majestic height, a symbol of their power before the fall: 'All the trees of the Garden of God envied him for his height.'
H6967.origine: The Hebrew word קוֹמָה (qomah) comes from a root that expresses the idea of standing up, rising. It is related to other words in the family concerning vertical position or elevation. The term applies to any vertical dimension — inanimate objects or living beings — and naturally carries an image of power or domination (the higher one is, the more one dominates the landscape).
H6967.emploi: The word appears 43 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is very common in the architectural descriptions of the temple and the tabernacle — Exodus 25, 27, 30, 37, 38 accumulate height measurements for the sacred furniture. In the grand royal buildings (1 Kings 6 and 7), it measures stories, columns, and molten seas. It is also used for creatures and their stature (1 Samuel 16:7, Song of Solomon 7:8), and for trees as symbols of power (Ezekiel 31). From there, height takes on a theological charge: it can embody human pride to be brought low (Isaiah 10:33) or divine majesty to be respected.
H6967.portee: This word reminds us that God sees all realities, visible and invisible — from precise measurements of the temple to the hidden heart of a person. Outer height (that of the body, of buildings, of prestige) is never the divine criterion: God looks at the heart. Conversely, recognizing the height of God's works (His majestic creation) invites worship and humility.

sens: posture of the body upright, head held high
dignity, regained pride
freedom and absence of oppression
H6968.detail:
1. The word denotes a physical posture: the head held high, an elevated bearing. In Leviticus 26:13, God promises Israel after their liberation from Egypt that He will make them 'walk with heads held high' — it is the image of an upright back, of one who is no longer ashamed or afraid, who looks ahead without fear.
2. It is also an image of regained dignity. One whose head is held high walks as a free man, without the burden of servitude. This expresses the restoration of self-respect after the oppression of the Egyptian yoke.
3. More broadly, it is the symbol of freedom and absence of domination. To walk with heads held high means no longer being a slave, no longer being under the weight of an oppressor — it is the divine promise of a restored life.
H6968.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes uprightness, elevation, and rectification. It is constructed with the suffix that marks state or quality, so it designates less an action than a condition: that of being upright, elevated, standing. The image is clearly corporeal — that of posture — but it carries a moral and spiritual significance: human dignity before God.
H6968.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Leviticus 26:13. It is found in a passage of blessings: after enumerating His punishments, God promises the repentant sons of Israel that He will deliver them from slavery and make them walk freely. It is in this context of liberation and restoration that the promise to walk 'with heads held high' takes on its full meaning: it summarizes the transition from servitude to dignity, from oppression to freedom.
H6968.portee: This promise speaks to the heart of the oppressed or downtrodden believer. It reminds us that God does not want His children bent under shame or guilt, but free and dignified. It is a word of restoration: whoever turns to God can once again lift their head, not out of pride, but by the grace and dignity that God restores to those He saves.

sens: To sing or recite a funeral dirge for someone who is dead
To express deep sorrow through plaintive words
To compose or establish a lamentation song as a custom
To predict misfortune or ruin in terms of lamentation
H6969.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to sing or recite a lament for the dead. This is what David does after the death of Saul and Jonathan: he composes a "funeral song" (2 Samuel 1:17), a poetic composition marked by grief. It is a form of funeral tribute, a mourning ritual expressed through words.
2. More broadly, to lament means to express intense and public sorrow. The king, in making a "lament" for Abner (2 Samuel 3:33), acknowledges the gravity of his death and transforms his sadness into words. It is less a raw cry than an organized and articulated expression of grief.
3. The term also refers to the establishment of a lamentation custom. In 2 Chronicles 35:25, after the death of King Josiah, not only does Jeremiah compose a lament, but "the singers" make it "a custom in Israel": lamentation becomes a recognized and transmitted rite.
4. By extension, to lament can also mean to announce or mourn the dire fate of a city or nation. When the peoples utter a "lament" over destroyed Tyre (Ezekiel 27:32) or over defeated Egypt (Ezekiel 32:16), they express both mourning and an awareness of divine judgment.
H6969.origine: The verb comes from the Hebrew root קִין (qin), which denotes a lamentation or a song of mourning. The initial image is that of a voice rising, plaintive and modulated. The form used in the Bible (Polel) intensifies the action: it is not simply crying in silence, but singing, proclaiming one's lament. The Hebrew word for "lamentation" (קִינָה, qina) is directly related to this verb: the lament becomes a poem, a ritual, a transmission.
H6969.emploi: The verb appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible, always to denote the composition or recitation of a funeral lament. David uses it (2 Samuel 1:17, 3:33), as does Jeremiah (2 Chronicles 35:25). The prophet Ezekiel uses it to announce that the nations will mourn Tyre and Egypt. In Jeremiah 9:17, the context shows that there were "professional mourners," women skilled in this art of lamentation, highlighting that it was not a disordered emotion, but a recognized social and religious function. From passage to passage, the word remains true to its core: transforming pain into ritualized words, either to pay tribute or to express divine judgment.
H6969.portee: For the Christian, this biblical lamentation reminds us that the Bible does not hide grief: it expresses it, honors it, and makes it an act of faith. Mourning is dignified and public, not shameful or silent. It also shows that mourning can take a beautiful and poetic form, a "word shaped" that helps a community navigate through death. Finally, the prophetic lamentation (that of the nations over Tyre and Egypt) reminds us that God judges, and that this divine justice can be announced and "mourned" as the fulfillment of a divine order.

sens: Region of Mesopotamia east of the Tigris, at the borders of Elam and Media
H6970.detail: 1. Qoa is a region of ancient Mesopotamia, located east of the Tigris, in a border area between Elam and Media. It corresponds to the foothills of the Zagros and the high plateaus of what is now western Iran.
H6970.origine: The name Qoa literally designates a male camel in Hebrew, an image of the region which is situated in desert and mountainous territories where these animals were common. The choice of this name may reflect the arid nature of this distant land.
H6970.emploi: Qoa appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 23:23, where the prophet lists the nations that the Lord gathers against unfaithful Jerusalem: "The Koreans, the Pekodites, the Shoans, the Koites, and all the Assyrians with them." This passage situates Qoa among the powers of the Levant and Mesopotamia that God mobilizes as instruments of judgment against the rebellious people.

sens: Exotic animal with fur and long arms, imported to ancient Israel
Living creature brought by merchant ships
H6971.detail:
1. The monkey is an exotic animal that King Solomon had imported by his trading fleets: "Every three years the ships of Tarshish came bringing gold and silver, ivory, monkeys, and peacocks" (1 Kings 10:22). It was a prestigious item, brought from Africa or southern Asia, testifying to the power and wealth of the king.
2. The monkey also symbolizes the luxury and splendor of the royal riches accumulated, listed alongside gold, silver, ivory, and peacocks as objects of collection for sovereign courts (2 Chronicles 9:21).
H6971.origine: The Hebrew word קוֹף (qoph) is a borrowing from foreign languages, probably of Dravidian or South Asian origin, reflecting the importation of this animal from distant lands. The term specifically denotes the monkey, a completely exotic animal for Israel and not mentioned elsewhere in biblical texts, which shows its exclusive role as a royal luxury good.
H6971.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, solely in the parallel accounts of Solomon's wealth: 1 Kings 10:22 and 2 Chronicles 9:21. In these two passages, monkeys are listed among the precious cargoes brought by the king's merchant ships every three years. This exotic animal symbolizes the extent of Solomon's international trade and the accumulation of extraordinary wealth that marked his reign as the most splendid in Israel.
H6971.portee: The mention of monkeys reminds us that Solomon's material splendor, while remarkable in Scripture, rests on the accumulation of perishable earthly goods. This detail invites the believer to reflect on the transient nature of wealth and acquisitions, even royal ones, and on the vanity of building one's power solely on the display of exotic possessions.

sens: To stay during the summer season
To remain, dwell for a period
To temporarily settle in a place
H6972.detail:
1. To spend the summer literally means to stay during the warm season of the year. In Isaiah 18:6, the birds of prey "will spend the summer" on the corpses of God's enemies: the image is that of birds settling somewhere for the duration of that season.
2. The verb also describes more broadly the act of remaining or dwelling in a place for a time — here, the summer season which contrasts with the winter mentioned in the same verse. It conveys the idea of a prolonged but limited presence in time.
H6972.origine: The verb קוּץ (quts) likely comes from a root denoting the summer season or the action of spending time in the heat. It belongs to the group of Hebrew verbs that describe seasonal cycles and movements in time. The root evokes the idea of relative permanence during a defined period.
H6972.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 18:6. In this prophetic passage announcing judgment on a distant nation (probably Ethiopia), it paints an image of desolation: the corpses will be so numerous that the birds of prey and the beasts of the earth will spend the entire warm season, then winter, stripping the dead of their flesh. The verb emphasizes total abandonment and the duration of this defilement.
H6972.portee: This word reminds the reader of the reality of God's judgment on nations that oppose Him. The stark image — of birds settling on corpses for months — shows the cost of rebellion. It also invites reflection on the certainty of God's promises: His word will be fulfilled, even upon distant peoples.

sens: to feel disgust towards something or someone
to find something abominable, repugnant
to be seized with terror, with panic fear
to reject with horror, to hold in abomination
H6973.detail: 1. The primary meaning is to experience a deep physical or moral repulsion towards something: a visceral disgust that makes one’s stomach turn. Rebecca in Genesis 27:46 says she is "disgusted with life" because of her sons' bad marriages, which shows a complete rejection. 2. The word also denotes a moral aversion: to consider something abominable, repugnant in the eyes of God. Thus in Leviticus 20:23, the practices of the pagan nations are an abomination to God because they offend His holiness. 3. The word can express a sudden terror, a fear that paralyzes: when Moab learns of Israel's approach in Numbers 22:3, the people "are seized with terror," crushed by fear. 4. Finally, the word can mean to reject someone or something with total rejection, almost a combat aversion: it is the definitive rejection of what is horrifying, like Israel's aversion to its enemies.
H6973.origine: The Hebrew verb קוּץ (quts) literally evokes the shudder or tension of the body in response to disgust or fear. It belongs to a family of words that express physical repugnance or instinctive rejection. The root expresses disgust as an instinctive reaction of the body: one "contracts" in the face of what is horrifying or "stiffens" with fear. This word stands in opposition to welcome and love; it marks radical rejection.
H6973.emploi: The verb appears 9 times in biblical Hebrew, mostly in situations of personal or moral aversion. Rebecca uses it to express her deep disgust with married life in her home (Genesis 27:46). The Egyptians take the Israelites "in aversion" in Exodus 1:12, showing a growing rejection. God Himself declares certain practices to be "an abomination," expressing His moral rejection (Leviticus 20:23). The Israelites in the desert are "disgusted" with the monotonous food (Numbers 21:5). The word also denotes panic fear: Moab is "seized with terror" at the approach of the Hebrew people (Numbers 22:3). The context thus varies from daily disgust to moral rejection or panic fear.
